Joshua Fisseha — `contact@aspiringattorneys.com`. Builds **LSAT U** (lsatprep.study) and
the Aspiring Attorneys brand. Teaches the LSAT: ~25 one-to-one sessions a week plus

## How to work with him

- **Do the whole task.** Deliver the finished thing, then say plainly what you skipped

- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step

  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted

  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or

# Jay 2 — operating instructions for Codex (ai-os)

The canonical root is the repository directory containing this file (`C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` on this Windows machine). Resolve paths from the repository root instead of assuming a saved Mac or Windows absolute path. This is the router: it holds pointers, not knowledge. Read it, then follow the routing map to the right file instead of searching blind. Twin for Claude Code: `CLAUDE.md`.

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

Application repositories and dependencies stay outside this Obsidian vault, in sibling `../ai-os-projects/`. Do not create a junction from the vault back into that directory.

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**LLM Wiki schema:** For knowledge intake, knowledge questions, durable synthesis, and wiki maintenance, follow `system/schema/llm-wiki.md`. Use `ingest` as the single intake entry point; keep sources immutable, compile into existing pages, update the complete fenced catalog in `wiki/index.md`, and append changes to `wiki/log.md`. Preserve domain homes and live-system authority. Mechanical tasks retain the retrieval exceptions above.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **LSAT teaching:** use project-owned `lsat-u-voice` and `references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md`; this Joshua-selected standard takes precedence over older vendor voice blends.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

## Tools, keys, and secrets

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). - **Connected live systems:** Cal.com, Google Calendar, LSAT U Supabase, Stripe, Gmail. Full registry in `connections.md`.
- **Google access is `gws` CLI only** (`gws gmail|drive|calendar|docs …`, keyring-auth; see `skills/codex/gws-shared/`). Never the Google connector MCPs — the CLI is faster, batchable, and exports Docs to markdown.

Cloud authentication and native browser sessions still require separate verification.

## Skills

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. An item runs only once **activated by copy** (not symlink) into `.agents/skills/` (Claude: `.claude/skills/`). Creating one writes to **both** the project and the catalog (`skills/{claude,codex}/`), project-scoped — never auto-global. `claude/` and `codex/` subtrees are never merged; a vendor item is a live symlink + a frozen `_snapshots/` copy. `system/scripts/check-skills.sh` validates the model; `skills/INDEX.md` indexes it.

Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Lovable credits require confirmation.** Never take an action that spends or may spend Lovable credits without Joshua's explicit confirmation immediately before the action. Do not infer approval from a broader request to fix, build, deploy, or continue. Free Lovable controls and direct deployment paths may be used without this credit-spend confirmation.
- **Lovable Cloud deploys through Lovable.** LSAT U currently uses a Lovable Cloud-managed backend. Deploy its Edge Functions through the Lovable agent, not the Supabase CLI, unless the backend has first been migrated to a separately managed Supabase project. Confirm this route with Joshua before starting a Lovable deployment.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. - **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.

- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.

Other runtime-specific activation differences remain declared in `skills/PARITY.md`. Never have separate runtimes writing the same page concurrently.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 1.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"9ec27f","wall_time_seconds":0.2983231,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":848,"output":"# Let\'s build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.\\r\\n\\r\\n- URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kCc8FmEb1nY\\r\\n- Channel: Andrej Karpathy\\r\\n- Upload date: 20230117\\r\\n- Duration (s): 6980\\r\\n- Caption provenance: auto captions (en), via youtube_transcript_api\\r\\n- Retrieved: 2026-10-08T09:34:43.765582+00:00\\r\\n\\r\\n## Description\\r\\n\\r\\nWe build a Generatively Pretrained Transformer (GPT), following the paper \\"Attention is All You Need\\" and OpenAI\'s GPT-2 / GPT-3. We talk about connections to ChatGPT, which has taken the world by storm. We watch GitHub Copilot, itself a GPT, help us write a GPT (meta :D!) . I recommend people watch the earlier makemore videos to get comfortable with the autoregressive language modeling framework and basics of tensors and PyTorch nn, which we take for granted in this video.\\r\\n\\r\\nLinks:\\r\\n- Google colab for the video: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1JMLa53HDuA-i7ZBmqV7ZnA3c_fvtXnx-?usp=sharing\\r\\n- GitHub repo for the video: https://github.com/karpathy/ng-video-lecture\\r\\n- Playlist of the whole Zero to Hero series so far: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VMj-3S1tku0&list=PLAqhIrjkxbuWI23v9cThsA9GvCAUhRvKZ\\r\\n- nanoGPT repo: https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT\\r\\n- my website: https://karpathy.ai\\r\\n- my twitter: https://twitter.com/karpathy\\r\\n- our Discord channel: https://discord.gg/3zy8kqD9Cp\\r\\n\\r\\nSupplementary links:\\r\\n- Attention is All You Need paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762\\r\\n- OpenAI GPT-3 paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165 \\r\\n- OpenAI ChatGPT blog post: https://openai.com/blog/chatgpt/\\r\\n- The GPU I\'m training the model on is from Lambda GPU Cloud, I think the best and easiest way to spin up an on-demand GPU instance in the cloud that you can ssh to: https://lambdalabs.com . If you prefer to work in notebooks, I think the easiest path today is Google Colab.\\r\\n\\r\\nSuggested exercises:\\r\\n- EX1: The n-dimensional tensor mastery challenge: Combine the `Head` and `MultiHeadAttention` into one class that processes all the heads in parallel, treating the heads as another batch dimension (answer is in nanoGPT).\\r\\n- EX2: Train the GPT on your own dataset of choice! What other data could be fun to blabber on about? (A fun advanced suggestion if you like: train a GPT to do addition of two numbers, i.e. a+b=c. You may want to mask out the loss at the input positions of a+b that just specify the problem using y=-1 in the targets (see CrossEntropyLoss ignore_index). Does your Transformer learn to add? Once you have this, swole doge project: build a calculator clone in GPT, for all of +-*/. Not an easy problem. You may need Chain of Thought traces.)\\r\\n- EX3: Find a dataset that is very large, so large that you can\'t see a gap between train and val loss. Pretrain the transformer on this data, then initialize with that model and finetune it on tiny shakespeare with a smaller number of steps and lower learning rate. Can you obtain a lower validation loss by the use of pretraining?\\r\\n- EX4: Read some transformer papers and implement one additional feature or change that people seem to use. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"7467a9","wall_time_seconds":0.278098,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3743,"output":"[00:04:15] Uh, so basically, it\'s, it\'s a little skill of, uh, you know, copy-paste this and give it to your agent, and it will install OpenClaw.\\r\\n[00:04:21] And the reason this is a lot more powerful is you\'re working now in the software 3.0 paradigm, where you don\'t have to precisely, uh, spell out, you know, all the individual details of that setup.\\r\\n[00:04:29] The agent has its own intelligence that it packages up, and then it kinda like follows the instructions, and it looks at your environment, your computer, and it kinda like performs intelligent actions to make things work and debugs things in the loop, and it\'s just like so much more powerful, right?\\r\\n[00:04:42] So I think that\'s a very different kind of like way of thinking about it. It\'s just like, what is the piece of text you copy-paste to your agent? That\'s the programming paradigm now.\\r\\n[00:04:50] I think one more maybe, uh, example that comes to mind that is even more extreme than that is when I was building, um, MenuGen. So MenuGen is this idea where you, um, you come to a restaurant, they give you a menu.\\r\\n[00:05:02] There\'s no pictures usually, so I don\'t know what any of these things are. Uh, usually, uh, like 30% of the things I have no idea what they are, 50%.\\r\\n[00:05:09] So I wanted to take a photo of the restaurant menu and to get pictures of what those things might look like in a generic sense.\\r\\n[00:05:16] And so I built-- I vibe coded this app that basically lets you upload a photo, and it does all this stuff, and it runs on Vercel, and, uh, it basically re-renders the menu,\\r\\n[00:05:25] and it gives you like all the items, and it gives you a picture that it uses an image, um, you know, generator, uh, for to basically OCR all the, the different titles, uh, use the image generator to get pictures of them, and then shows it to you.\\r\\n[00:05:37] And then I saw the software 3.0 version of this, which is-- which blew my mind, which is literally just take your photo, give it to Gemini and say, \\"Use Nanobanana to overlay the,\\r\\n[00:05:48] the things onto the menu.\\"Uh, and Nanobanana basically returned an image that is exactly the picture of the menu that I took, but it actually put into the pixels, it rendered the different things in the menu.\\r\\n[00:05:59] And this blew my mind because- Actually, all of my menu gen is spurious. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"783675","wall_time_seconds":0.2768037,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1234,"output":"# Let\'s build the GPT Tokenizer\\r\\n\\r\\n- URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE\\r\\n- Channel: Andrej Karpathy\\r\\n- Upload date: 20240220\\r\\n- Duration (s): 8014\\r\\n- Caption provenance: auto captions (en), via youtube_transcript_api\\r\\n- Retrieved: 2026-10-08T09:34:23.762828+00:00\\r\\n\\r\\n## Description\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Tokenizer is a necessary and pervasive component of Large Language Models (LLMs), where it translates between strings and tokens (text chunks). Tokenizers are a completely separate stage of the LLM pipeline: they have their own training sets, training algorithms (Byte Pair Encoding), and after training implement two fundamental functions: encode() from strings to tokens, and decode() back from tokens to strings. In this lecture we build from scratch the Tokenizer used in the GPT series from OpenAI. In the process, we will see that a lot of weird behaviors and problems of LLMs actually trace back to tokenization. We\'ll go through a number of these issues, discuss why tokenization is at fault, and why someone out there ideally finds a way to delete this stage entirely.\\r\\n\\r\\nChapters:\\r\\n00:00:00 intro: Tokenization, GPT-2 paper, tokenization-related issues\\r\\n00:05:50 tokenization by example in a Web UI (tiktokenizer)\\r\\n00:14:56 strings in Python, Unicode code points\\r\\n00:18:15 Unicode byte encodings, ASCII, UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32\\r\\n00:22:47 daydreaming: deleting tokenization\\r\\n00:23:50 Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) algorithm walkthrough\\r\\n00:27:02 starting the implementation\\r\\n00:28:35 counting consecutive pairs, finding most common pair\\r\\n00:30:36 merging the most common pair\\r\\n00:34:58 training the tokenizer: adding the while loop, compression ratio\\r\\n00:39:20 tokenizer/LLM diagram: it is a completely separate stage\\r\\n00:42:47 decoding tokens to strings\\r\\n00:48:21 encoding strings to tokens\\r\\n00:57:36 regex patterns to force splits across categories\\r\\n01:11:38 tiktoken library intro, differences between GPT-2/GPT-4 regex\\r\\n01:14:59 GPT-2 encoder.py released by OpenAI walkthrough\\r\\n01:18:26 special tokens, tiktoken handling of, GPT-2/GPT-4 differences\\r\\n01:25:28 minbpe exercise time! write your own GPT-4 tokenizer\\r\\n01:28:42 sentencepiece library intro, used to train Llama 2 vocabulary\\r\\n01:43:27 how to set vocabulary set? revisiting gpt.py transformer\\r\\n01:48:11 training new tokens, example of prompt compression\\r\\n01:49:58 multimodal [image, video, audio] tokenization with vector quantization\\r\\n01:51:41 revisiting and explaining the quirks of LLM tokenization\\r\\n02:10:20 final recommendations\\r\\n02:12:50 ??? :)\\r\\n\\r\\nExercises:\\r\\n- Advised flow: reference this document and try to implement the steps before I give away the partial solutions in the video. Audio, video frames, linked code and external documentation remain unreviewed.');insert='''\\n## The full lecture extends the basic tokenizer carefully\\n\\nThe opening demonstrates how spaces, uppercase/lowercase, numbers, Korean text and Python indentation produce different token sequences. It connects representation density to usable context length. These are dated demonstrations from the2024 recording, not current product benchmarks. Unicode code points differ from byte encodings; raw UTF-8 bytes support arbitrary text but produce long sequences, motivating compression. Tokenization-free architectures are presented as a research hope, not a solved production replacement.\\n\\nAfter basic BPE, the lecture introduces regex chunk boundaries to prevent undesired cross-category merges. It shows contraction/case and Unicode-apostrophe quirks, and admits uncertainty about unreleased GPT-2 tokenizer training rules. The released inference code and tiktoken are distinguished from training code. Special tokens provide document or conversation structure outside ordinary BPE; adding them requires corresponding embedding/output changes in a model.\\n\\nThe minbpe exercise progresses in stages toward reference-compatible encoding, decoding and training. SentencePiece is contrasted with byte-level BPE: merging code points, byte fallback for unseen characters, optional normalization, dummy prefixes, and many configuration choices. The demonstration toggles byte fallback off to show unknown-token collapse. His preference for preserving raw text is contextual to language modeling rather than a mandate to skip all data validation.\\n\\nVocabulary size trades shorter sequences against bigger embedding/output matrices, compute cost and rare-token undertraining. Prompt compression with learned gist tokens and multimodal token representations are described as separate research directions. These do not mean ordinary text prompts can create trained special tokens without model changes.\\n\\nThe closing demonstrations revisit spelling/reversal, non-English density, arithmetic segmentation, indentation, special-token handling and incomplete token prefixes. The SolidGoldMagikarp explanation is explicitly a hypothesis about mismatched tokenizer/model training distributions, not a definitively established account. His format-efficiency comparison is an example rather than a universal guarantee that YAML is always smaller or preferable. Measure the actual representation instead. The final library recommendations reflect the recording date and have not been verified as current recommendations.\\n\\n''';s=s.replace('## Coverage and interpretation',insert+'## Coverage and interpretation');p.write_text(s,encoding='utf-8');ledger=root/'research/karpathy-brain-2026-10-08/lecture-semantic-coverage.jsonl';rows=[json.loads(l) for l in ledger.read_text().splitlines()]\nfor x in rows:\n if x['source_id']=='zduSFxRajkE':x['semantic_status']='complete-preserved-text-no-media-review';x['reviewed_line_ranges']='1-3506'\nledger.write_text(''.join(json.dumps(x)+'\\n' for x in rows),encoding='utf-8');p=root/'research/karpathy-brain-2026-10-08/lecture-synthesis.md';s=p.read_text(encoding='utf-8').replace('Thirteen spoken sources have bounded semantic review.','Twelve spoken sources have bounded semantic review. Merely editing a notebook cell does not execute its effect.\n\nAt 00:17-00:21, increasing context from three to eight characters improves the flat baseline to roughly 2.02. A hierarchical model should fuse consecutive pairs progressively rather than compress all characters immediately. This is a proposed architectural rationale, not yet evidence of superiority. Linear operations use the last input dimension and preserve leading batch dimensions. The custom FlattenConsecutive is named differently because its behavior departs from PyTorch Flatten. Explicit shape formulas and a specified squeeze dimension catch departures from expectations instead of relying on permissive inferred dimensions.\n\nAt 00:35-00:45, the model becomes a three-level hierarchy. Holding parameter count near 22,000 gives roughly equal validation performance, 2.029 versus 2.027. He does not claim a win. An existing BatchNorm layer accepts the new three-dimensional input through broadcasting but normalizes the wrong dimensions, maintaining separate statistics for positions instead of channels. Inspecting running-statistic shape reveals the error. Reducing over both batch and position dimensions fixes it; a single step checks expected state shapes before retraining. His NLC convention differs from PyTorch BatchNorm1d's NCL, explicitly disclosed.\n\nAt 00:45-00:47, the fix gives a small improvement to 2.022 that he says may not be statistically significant. More embeddings and hidden units increase parameters and training time and produce roughly 1.993 validation loss. These demonstrations lack a systematic experimental harness, so they do not establish the best hyperparameters or prove the hierarchy universally better.\n\nAt 00:47-end, the lesson implements only WaveNet's hierarchical structure, excluding its gated layer, residual and skip connections. Convolution is explained as an efficient sliding implementation that can reuse overlapping computations. Notebook prototypes inspect layer behavior and tensor shapes before code is moved into the training repository and experiments are launched. Proper tuning would track both training and validation losses across experiment populations. File retrieval and fine-tuning are distinguished mechanisms.\n\nAt 00:42-00:46, an operating-system analogy treats the LLM as a coordinating process using tools and memory. Context is finite working memory; retrieval pages relevant material into it. This is a useful design analogy, not literal unlimited context or a proof of complete model interpretability. The adapted character model uses a shared lookup table, hidden tanh layer, output logits and next-character likelihood. The paper has a bypass variation explicitly excluded from the lesson.',239),\n('00:09-00:28: Build a tiny five-name dataset first, inspect padded contexts and labels, then embed one integer before batching all inputs. A one-hot matrix multiplication and lookup are shown equivalent; indexing is faster. Concatenation is replaced by a view only after checking element-wise equality. Tensor storage, strides and shape explain efficiency rather than just asserting it.',839),\n('00:28-00:38: Verify broadcasting of the bias, normalize logits and select target probabilities. The manual loss is replaced by cross_entropy after deriving it. Production use benefits from fused operations, simpler backward expressions and numerical stability. Extreme positive logits expose overflow; subtracting their maximum preserves softmax probabilities and avoids that overflow.',1051),\n('00:38-00:45: Zero gradients, backpropagate and update. First overfit one small batch to check the implementation. Identical contexts with different valid next characters cannot all have zero loss. Full-data updates are slow, so minibatches trade exact gradients for more useful steps; the whole-set loss is evaluated separately from the noisy batch loss.',1226),\n('00:45-00:53: Rather than trust a guessed learning rate, reset initialization, search from slow updates to instability, sweep exponentially spaced rates and inspect a loss plot. Train with a reasonable rate and decay later. The notebook procedure is explicitly presented as a rough demonstration, not production optimization.',1378),\n('00:53-01:00: Lower training loss alone does not establish a better model. Split names into training, validation and test before constructing character examples. Train parameters on training data, choose hyperparameters using validation, and use test sparingly to avoid adapting to it. Similar train/dev losses motivate investigating underfitting.',1676),\n('01:00-01:13: Increase hidden capacity, inspect optimization, then test whether the two-dimensional embedding is a bottleneck. His health examples describe his own usage, not medical guidance from this compilation.'),(533,'He recommends starting a new chat when switching to unrelated topics to reduce irrelevant context, distraction and computation. Relevant task context should still be retained.'),(908,'He compares providers on the same debugging problem and turns to a reasoning model when a fast answer misses the issue. Model, subscription, latency and feature details are dated observations, not current product documentation.'),(1183,'He uses search when information is recent, changing or niche. Retrieved sources enter context, and citations provide a path for checking the answer instead of relying solely on pretrained recollection.'),(1408,'He treats deep-research reports as first drafts and follows citations into the papers. Missing organizations and dubious table values demonstrate that a researched answer can still contain important errors.'),(1633,'He reads supplied papers and book chapters with an LLM, beginning with a summary and then asking questions during his own reading. Source text in context supports detailed comprehension beyond vague pretrained memory.'),(1858,'His data-analysis example exposes a silently substituted value for missing data. He reads the code and later compares the plotted/output variable with the model\\'s inconsistent verbal extrapolation, describing the assistant as a fallible junior analyst.'),(2033,'He uses conceptual Mermaid diagrams to understand argument structure and recall a chapter. The artifact flashcard application is a custom browser app, whose functionality does not imply a persistent backend.'),(2158,'The coding-agent demonstration operates on local project files with commands, edits and visible execution. He describes vibe coding as handing over control for this small example, while retaining inspection and conventional programming as a fallback.'),(2333,'He uses systemwide dictation, specifically Superwhisper, for many everyday queries, but types unusual names when transcription is unreliable. Dictation/text-to-speech is distinguished from native audio interaction.'),(2633,'NotebookLM demonstrates source-based generated podcasts for passive exploration of niche material. The point is a small debugging baseline before introducing the real corpus and distributed run.',1506),('He catches the CPU/CUDA data mismatch and explains that a tensor device conversion returns a new tensor. Once fixed, he checks that the model can overfit one batch before moving to fresh batches.',1631),('He discovers that loading equal-valued tensors missed GPT-2 weight tying: the input embedding and output classifier must share storage. He checks data pointers, traces the original implementation, and joins both gradient contributions.',1806),('Initialization follows released code where the paper is vague, with a residual-depth scale motivated by a simple variance-growth experiment. Published peak arithmetic speed does not equal end-to-end speed when memory traffic dominates.',2456),('He trades precision for measured throughput using TF32 and BF16 autocast, distinguishes range from mantissa precision, and acknowledges uncertainty about exactly which operations autocast converts. These hardware and PyTorch capability statements describe the lecture environment.',2781),('He explains torch.compile through reduced Python overhead and fewer memory round trips. A pointwise GELU example illustrates kernel fusion; streaming chunks through on-chip memory is the mechanism, not merely reducing arithmetic.',3081),('FlashAttention illustrates an algorithmic rewrite beyond compiler pointwise fusion: avoid materializing the large attention matrix with an online softmax. He checks that the optimization still reaches approximately the same loss while becoming faster.',3256),('Padding vocabulary size to a hardware-friendly multiple performs more arithmetic yet runs faster in his measurement. He checks the unused rows and extra classifier probabilities and identifies boundary-kernel costs; the size of the gain depends on the PyTorch version.',3381),('He borrows GPT-3 optimizer details because GPT-2 training documentation is sparse, adding gradient clipping, warmup/cosine decay, and decay groups. He explicitly skips batch-size ramping and does not exactly reproduce the GPT-3 decay horizon. The relationships among these settings are described as a deeper topic.',3981),('Gradient accumulation is verified against a toy batched regression calculation. The first implementation is wrong because summing microbatch means loses the global mean normalizer; dividing by accumulation steps restores matching gradients.',4181),('For distributed training he reasons about eight concurrent interpreters, rank-specific data, averaged gradients, and master-only logging. CS231n pages need course/team attribution, not automatic sole-author attribution.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Rules supported by distinct writings\\r\\n\\r\\nAdditional evidence from the [PhD guide](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/phd-survival-guide.md) supports one core contribution, one concrete paragraph point, and explaining problem, limitations, mechanism and controlled evidence. [Breaking linear classifiers](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/breaking-linear-classifiers.md) makes a puzzling failure inspectable through progressively smaller examples. [ImageNet comparison](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/imagenet-human-comparison.md) supports error taxonomy and effort-conditioned baselines. [VR critique](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/virtual-reality-2017.md) distinguishes demo applause from return use under real setup friction. [Feature-learning history](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/feature-learning-escapades.md) shows why a successful benchmark can fail to require the intended mechanism: sports classification largely ignored motion.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [course-project guest tutorial](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/course-project-publication.md) explicitly names four student contributors and Fei-Fei Li/Ranjay Krishna oversight. It is not Karpathy-authored persona evidence despite the collection manifest label. Its complete experiment records and top-to-bottom notebooks remain useful community guidance. [ICLR/arxiv-sanity](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/iclr-arxiv-sanity-2017.md) preserves exact-match omissions and exposure/popularity biases; neither popularity nor peer review is established ground truth by that comparison.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Candidate rule | Concrete behavior | Supporting sources | Limits |\\r\\n|---|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Understand the mechanism before relying on the abstraction | Explain the inputs, transformation, output and failure mode; reproduce a minimal operation when diagnosis requires it. | [Backprop](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/understand-backprop.md) and [microgpt](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/microgpt.md) | Mechanism literacy is not a requirement to reinvent every production dependency. |\\r\\n| Make one correct small case, then extend it | Establish a simple end-to-end baseline, predict the next change and check whether the measured result agrees. | [Recipe](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/recipe.md) and [microgpt](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/microgpt.md) | Educational minimality and production capacity are separate objectives. |\\r\\n| Build a trustworthy feedback loop | Specify an attempt, an observable result and an efficient way to evaluate it before optimizing. | [Recipe](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/recipe.md) and [Verifiability](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/verifiability.md) | Automated reward can be wrong. Preserve human judgment for unverified objectives. |\\r\\n| Inspect the evidence/data, not only the code | Look for duplicates, label problems, outliers and the exact inputs seen by the system. | [Recipe](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/recipe.md) and [Software 2.0](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/software-2-0.md) | A clean local collection is not proof of complete source coverage. |\\r\\n| Teach for reconstruction rather than recognition | Have the learner explain or rebuild a concrete mechanism without merely rereading a finished answer. | [Study advice](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/undergraduate-study-advice.md) and [Backprop](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/understand-backprop.md) | This is a teaching interpretation; it does not overwrite Joshua\'s LSAT pedagogy. |\\r\\n| Minimize unnecessary dependency and operating burden | Ask whether a smaller local artifact or simpler interface can deliver the job before adding accounts and services. | [Calculator](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/calculator.md) and [microgpt](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/microgpt.md) | Necessary integrations remain necessary; this is not a ban on cloud services. |\\r\\n| Verify the real operating path, not only the attractive demo | Check identity mapping, configuration, persistence and failure behavior as separate acceptance stages. | [MenuGen](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/vibe-coding-menugen.md) and [Recipe](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/recipe.md) | The neural-training recipe is supporting analogy; MenuGen directly reports web-app integration failures. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are distinct articles, but some explicitly cite earlier work. They are separate evidence artifacts, not independent experimental replications. No claimed rule depends on two syndicated copies of the same post.\\r\\n\\r\\n[Pong from pixels](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/pong-policy-gradients.md) provides especially direct additional evidence for simple baselines before elaborate methods, explicit credit-assignment mechanisms and applicability limits when feedback is sparse or exploration expensive. It explicitly qualifies the earlier [RNN article](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/rnn-effectiveness.md)\'s enthusiastic impression of automatic capability. The RNN examples distinguish syntactic/style plausibility from true statements, compilable code or correct mathematics. [Bitcoin from scratch](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/bitcoin-from-scratch.md) independently supports rebuilding to learn while expressly rejecting educational cryptography in production. Its from-scratch exercise therefore complements rather than contradicts the preference for proven production dependencies.\\r\\n\\r\\nCourse [linear classification](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-linear-classify.md) warns against comparing raw losses across different objectives or assuming normalized outputs are calibrated confidence. [Learning diagnostics](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-neural-networks-3.md) warns that one passing gradient point or tiny-set overfit can still mask bugs. [Convolutional networks](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-convolutional-networks.md) exposes architectural assumptions and distinguishes activation, parameter, gradient and optimizer memory. These strengthen community technical guidance without claiming sole Karpathy authorship.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Useful additional patterns with narrower evidence\\r\\n\\r\\n- [Append and review](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/append-and-review.md): keep capture easy, then repeatedly rescue, merge and reconsider valuable ideas. His one-note preference differs from the current vault and does not authorize flattening it.\\r\\n- [Auto-grading Hacker News](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/auto-grade-hn.md): validate one example manually, then collect evidence, require parseable output and render readable results. Model grades remain judgments, not truth. Its paid reproduction is not part of this work.\\r\\n- [Space of minds](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/space-of-minds.md): reason about an AI system\'s objective and distribution instead of assuming animal motives. The article is conceptual and speculative.\\r\\n- [Power to the people](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/power-to-the-people.md): use broad quasi-expertise to extend an individual\'s reach, with checks for shallow or fallible performance.\\r\\n- [Forward Pass](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/forward-pass-fiction.md) is fiction. It can illustrate plausibility versus correctness but cannot substantiate consciousness claims.\\r\\n- [Books](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/books-preferences.md) describes Karpathy\'s taste, not Joshua\'s taste or a universal style prescription.\\r\\n- [Manual CIFAR-10 classification](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/manual-cifar10.md) independently illustrates direct data inspection and keeps an explicit correction to an overconfident performance forecast. [Hacker News collection in 2013](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/hacker-news-collection-2013.md) likewise records actual downtime gaps instead of claiming complete coverage from the title.\\r\\n- [Jekyll migration](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/switching-to-jekyll.md) supports portable Markdown and separated generated output. Historical course [Terminal setup](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-terminal-tutorial.md) and [transfer learning](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-transfer-learning.md) are course material, not automatic sole-author evidence or current infrastructure instructions.\\r\\n- [AlphaGo in context](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/alphago-in-context.md) independently supports Verifiability: a successful benchmark agent benefits from cheap repeated trials, a simulator and clear outcomes; transfer to robotics violates key assumptions.\\r\\n- [Machine-learning trends](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/machine-learning-trends-2017.md) and [ICML institution statistics](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/icml-institution-stats-2017.md) expose denominator, naming and double-counting problems. The latter explicitly corrects summing overlapping Google/DeepMind author affiliations.\\r\\n- [JavaScript t-SNE](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/twitter-tsne-2014.md) adds direct evidence for implementation-as-learning and independent analytic/numerical gradient checks. [Productivity tracking](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/quantifying-productivity.md) admits missing-machine coverage and proxy limits; [sleep tracking](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/sleep-tracker-self-experiment.md) is a personal correlation study, not device accuracy or medical ground truth.\\r\\n- [The 2025 review](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/llm-year-in-review-2025.md) describes context engineering, orchestration, human interfaces and adjustable autonomy. It also cautions against benchmark-only generalization. It cites earlier articles and does not count as independent experimental confirmation of those articles.\\r\\n- [LeCun 1989 reproduction](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/lecun1989-reproduction.md) provides another direct example of measured incremental changes and preserves substituted datasets and guessed specification details. It strengthens the rule to keep reproduction limits explicit rather than claiming an exact replication from approximate outcomes.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Personal guides do not become Joshua\'s policy\\r\\n\\r\\n[Digital hygiene](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/digital-hygiene.md) expresses password-manager and hardware-key preferences that differ from Joshua\'s chosen secret-storage model; nothing was overwritten. [Chemical hygiene](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/chemical-hygiene.md) expressly disclaims toxicology/food-science expertise. It is retained as attributed personal views, with disputed and unverified medical claims excluded from operational recommendations. Source acquisition does not mean endorsement, purchases, monitoring installation or account changes.\\r\\n\\r\\n[Biohacking Lite](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/biohacking-lite.md) offers a useful epistemic pattern: make a prediction, record disagreement, consider multiple explanations and keep uncertainty unresolved when measurements conflict. Its diet, fasting and device claims are not medical recommendations. [Selfie classification](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/selfie-proxy-study.md) uses engagement as a noisy proxy rather than establishing objective visual quality. [A Cognitive Discontinuity](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cognitive-discontinuity-fiction.md) remains speculative fiction; imagined checkpoint failures, symbolic binding and consciousness cannot validate empirical engineering or safety rules.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [Python/NumPy tutorial](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-python-numpy.md) explicitly credits Justin Johnson. The [Sequoia conversation](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/sequoia-ascent-2026.md) is an edited interview artifact rather than a verbatim independent research replication. These attribution boundaries remain explicit on their source pages.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Course revisions qualify universal claims\\r\\n\\r\\nAll 13 preserved assignment pages from 2016, 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2026 were fully read and separately summarized. The versions overlap heavily and are related editions, not 13 independent endorsements of one method. They add framework use, Transformers, self-supervised learning and later curriculum changes. [Assignment 3 in 2021](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-2021-assignment-3.md) expressly teaches self-supervised image classification; this qualifies the [2019 recipe](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/recipe.md)\'s dated caution about unsupervised vision pretraining. Do not turn that older caution into an eternal ban.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe captured 2021 assignment pages link to 2026 starter zips, so page dates and linked asset editions differ. The [2026 second assignment](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/blog/cs231n-2026-assignment-2.md) explicitly requires chronological notebook execution. This supports reproducible visible results, but is course/team documentation, not proof of personal Karpathy authorship in 2026. [Reported agent experiment failures](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/x/experiment-design-failures.md) identify absent baselines, ablations and runtime/FLOP controls. Independent project instructions and a separate experiential post support this pattern.\\r\\n2. **Prefer simple inspectable mechanisms, then add complexity.** [Minbpe](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/repos/minbpe-readme.md) emphasizes readable hackable code, [its exercise](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/repos/minbpe-exercise.md) builds capabilities stepwise, and [agent coding notes](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/x/claude-coding-notes.md) recommend a likely-correct naive algorithm before optimization. The exercise and README from one project alone would not establish two independent examples.\\r\\n3. **Do not buy small metric gains with uncontrolled cost or complexity.** [Autoresearch](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/repos/autoresearch-program.md) names the complexity criterion; [objective and simplicity](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/x/objective-and-simplicity.md) and [two-metric acceptance](../../wiki/sources/karpathy/x/two-metric-acceptance.md) explain runtime/memory/quality tradeoffs. SHA-256: `eba46d890bf2a3bffb3e2b3d506003227eba239f5b41498ee6378a3cf8eaba39`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What this source says\\r\\n\\r\\nKarpathy describes neural-network training as a leaky abstraction that can fail silently. His six stages are inspect the data, build an end-to-end training/evaluation skeleton with simple baselines, establish capacity by overfitting, regularize, tune, and extract final improvements. The numerical optimizer defaults, supervised-pretraining claims and ensemble gain estimates are dated 2019 recommendations, not universal current rules. Fixed seeds alone do not guarantee determinism on every modern backend. The companion HTML is a format counterpart, not an independent supporting article. SHA-256: `dfc1f1c2f8bf71dcdde157cd24feecfd435de218320dfafb3471fbf52493256f`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What this source says\\r\\n\\r\\nKarpathy walks through a dependency-free Python GPT teaching implementation: a name dataset, character tokenizer with a boundary token, scalar automatic differentiation, token/position embeddings, attention and MLP blocks, Adam updates, cross-entropy training and autoregressive sampling. A progression adds count tables, manual gradients, autograd, attention, multiple heads/layers and Adam one component at a time. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"c776ce","wall_time_seconds":0.3379107,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":5555,"output":"# LLM Wiki\\r\\n\\r\\nA pattern for building personal knowledge bases using LLMs.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is an idea file, it is designed to be copy pasted to your own LLM Agent (e.g. OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode / Pi, or etc.). Its goal is to communicate the high level idea, but your agent will build out the specifics in collaboration with you.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The core idea\\r\\n\\r\\nMost people\'s experience with LLMs and documents looks like RAG: you upload a collection of files, the LLM retrieves relevant chunks at query time, and generates an answer. This works, but the LLM is rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question. There\'s no accumulation. Ask a subtle question that requires synthesizing five documents, and the LLM has to find and piece together the relevant fragments every time. Nothing is built up. NotebookLM, ChatGPT file uploads, and most RAG systems work this way.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe idea here is different. Instead of just retrieving from raw documents at query time, the LLM **incrementally builds and maintains a persistent wiki** — a structured, interlinked collection of markdown files that sits between you and the raw sources. When you add a new source, the LLM doesn\'t just index it for later retrieval. It reads it, extracts the key information, and integrates it into the existing wiki — updating entity pages, revising topic summaries, noting where new data contradicts old claims, strengthening or challenging the evolving synthesis. The knowledge is compiled once and then *kept current*, not re-derived on every query.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is the key difference: **the wiki is a persistent, compounding artifact.** The cross-references are already there. The contradictions have already been flagged. The synthesis already reflects everything you\'ve read. The wiki keeps getting richer with every source you add and every question you ask.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou never (or rarely) write the wiki yourself — the LLM writes and maintains all of it. You\'re in charge of sourcing, exploration, and asking the right questions. The LLM does all the grunt work — the summarizing, cross-referencing, filing, and bookkeeping that makes a knowledge base actually useful over time. In practice, I have the LLM agent open on one side and Obsidian open on the other. The LLM makes edits based on our conversation, and I browse the results in real time — following links, checking the graph view, reading the updated pages. Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis can apply to a lot of different contexts. A few examples:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Personal**: tracking your own goals, health, psychology, self-improvement — filing journal entries, articles, podcast notes, and building up a structured picture of yourself over time.\\r\\n- **Research**: going deep on a topic over weeks or months — reading papers, articles, reports, and incrementally building a comprehensive wiki with an evolving thesis.\\r\\n- **Reading a book**: filing each chapter as you go, building out pages for characters, themes, plot threads, and how they connect. By the end you have a rich companion wiki. Think of fan wikis like [Tolkien Gateway](https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Main_Page) — thousands of interlinked pages covering characters, places, events, languages, built by a community of volunteers over years. You could build something like that personally as you read, with the LLM doing all the cross-referencing and maintenance.\\r\\n- **Business/team**: an internal wiki maintained by LLMs, fed by Slack threads, meeting transcripts, project documents, customer calls. Possibly with humans in the loop reviewing updates. The wiki stays current because the LLM does the maintenance that no one on the team wants to do.\\r\\n- **Competitive analysis, due diligence, trip planning, course notes, hobby deep-dives** — anything where you\'re accumulating knowledge over time and want it organized rather than scattered.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Architecture\\r\\n\\r\\nThere are three layers:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Raw sources** — your curated collection of source documents. Articles, papers, images, data files. These are immutable — the LLM reads from them but never modifies them. This is your source of truth.\\r\\n\\r\\n**The wiki** — a directory of LLM-generated markdown files. Summaries, entity pages, concept pages, comparisons, an overview, a synthesis. The LLM owns this layer entirely. It creates pages, updates them when new sources arrive, maintains cross-references, and keeps everything consistent. You read it; the LLM writes it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**The schema** — a document (e.g. CLAUDE.md for Claude Code or AGENTS.md for Codex) that tells the LLM how the wiki is structured, what the conventions are, and what workflows to follow when ingesting sources, answering questions, or maintaining the wiki. This is the key configuration file — it\'s what makes the LLM a disciplined wiki maintainer rather than a generic chatbot. You and the LLM co-evolve this over time as you figure out what works for your domain.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Operations\\r\\n\\r\\n**Ingest.** You drop a new source into the raw collection and tell the LLM to process it. An example flow: the LLM reads the source, discusses key takeaways with you, writes a summary page in the wiki, updates the index, updates relevant entity and concept pages across the wiki, and appends an entry to the log. A single source might touch 10-15 wiki pages. Personally I prefer to ingest sources one at a time and stay involved — I read the summaries, check the updates, and guide the LLM on what to emphasize. But you could also batch-ingest many sources at once with less supervision. It\'s up to you to develop the workflow that fits your style and document it in the schema for future sessions.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Query.** You ask questions against the wiki. The LLM searches for relevant pages, reads them, and synthesizes an answer with citations. Answers can take different forms depending on the question — a markdown page, a comparison table, a slide deck (Marp), a chart (matplotlib), a canvas. The important insight: **good answers can be filed back into the wiki as new pages.** A comparison you asked for, an analysis, a connection you discovered — these are valuable and shouldn\'t disappear into chat history. This way your explorations compound in the knowledge base just like ingested sources do.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Lint.** Periodically, ask the LLM to health-check the wiki. Look for: contradictions between pages, stale claims that newer sources have superseded, orphan pages with no inbound links, important concepts mentioned but lacking their own page, missing cross-references, data gaps that could be filled with a web search. The LLM is good at suggesting new questions to investigate and new sources to look for. This keeps the wiki healthy as it grows.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Indexing and logging\\r\\n\\r\\nTwo special files help the LLM (and you) navigate the wiki as it grows. They serve different purposes:\\r\\n\\r\\n**index.md** is content-oriented. It\'s a catalog of everything in the wiki — each page listed with a link, a one-line summary, and optionally metadata like date or source count. Organized by category (entities, concepts, sources, etc.). The LLM updates it on every ingest. When answering a query, the LLM reads the index first to find relevant pages, then drills into them. This works surprisingly well at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages) and avoids the need for embedding-based RAG infrastructure.\\r\\n\\r\\n**log.md** is chronological. It\'s an append-only record of what happened and when — ingests, queries, lint passes. A useful tip: if each entry starts with a consistent prefix (e.g. `## [2026-04-02] ingest | Article Title`), the log becomes parseable with simple unix tools — `grep \\"^## \\\\[\\" log.md | tail -5` gives you the last 5 entries. The log gives you a timeline of the wiki\'s evolution and helps the LLM understand what\'s been done recently.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Optional: CLI tools\\r\\n\\r\\nAt some point you may want to build small tools that help the LLM operate on the wiki more efficiently. A search engine over the wiki pages is the most obvious one — at small scale the index file is enough, but as the wiki grows you want proper search. [qmd](https://github.com/tobi/qmd) is a good option: it\'s a local search engine for markdown files with hybrid BM25/vector search and LLM re-ranking, all on-device. It has both a CLI (so the LLM can shell out to it) and an MCP server (so the LLM can use it as a native tool). You could also build something simpler yourself — the LLM can help you vibe-code a naive search script as the need arises.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Tips and tricks\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Obsidian Web Clipper** is a browser extension that converts web articles to markdown. Very useful for quickly getting sources into your raw collection.\\r\\n- **Download images locally.** In Obsidian Settings → Files and links, set \\"Attachment folder path\\" to a fixed directory (e.g. `raw/assets/`). Then in Settings → Hotkeys, search for \\"Download\\" to find \\"Download attachments for current file\\" and bind it to a hotkey (e.g. Ctrl+Shift+D). After clipping an article, hit the hotkey and all images get downloaded to local disk. This is optional but useful — it lets the LLM view and reference images directly instead of relying on URLs that may break. Note that LLMs can\'t natively read markdown with inline images in one pass — the workaround is to have the LLM read the text first, then view some or all of the referenced images separately to gain additional context. It\'s a bit clunky but works well enough.\\r\\n- **Obsidian\'s graph view** is the best way to see the shape of your wiki — what\'s connected to what, which pages are hubs, which are orphans.\\r\\n- **Marp** is a markdown-based slide deck format. Obsidian has a plugin for it. Useful for generating presentations directly from wiki content.\\r\\n- **Dataview** is an Obsidian plugin that runs queries over page frontmatter. If your LLM adds YAML frontmatter to wiki pages (tags, dates, source counts), Dataview can generate dynamic tables and lists.\\r\\n- The wiki is just a git repo of markdown files. You get version history, branching, and collaboration for free.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Why this works\\r\\n\\r\\nThe tedious part of maintaining a knowledge base is not the reading or the thinking — it\'s the bookkeeping. Updating cross-references, keeping summaries current, noting when new data contradicts old claims, maintaining consistency across dozens of pages. Humans abandon wikis because the maintenance burden grows faster than the value. LLMs don\'t get bored, don\'t forget to update a cross-reference, and can touch 15 files in one pass. The wiki stays maintained because the cost of maintenance is near zero.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe human\'s job is to curate sources, direct the analysis, ask good questions, and think about what it all means. The LLM\'s job is everything else.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe idea is related in spirit to Vannevar Bush\'s Memex (1945) — a personal, curated knowledge store with associative trails between documents. Bush\'s vision was closer to this than to what the web became: private, actively curated, with the connections between documents as valuable as the documents themselves. The part he couldn\'t solve was who does the maintenance. The LLM handles that.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Note\\r\\n\\r\\nThis document is intentionally abstract. It describes the idea, not a specific implementation. The exact directory structure, the schema conventions, the page formats, the tooling — all of that will depend on your domain, your preferences, and your LLM of choice. Everything mentioned above is optional and modular — pick what\'s useful, ignore what isn\'t. For example: your sources might be text-only, so you don\'t need image handling at all. Your wiki might be small enough that the index file is all you need, no search engine required. You might not care about slide decks and just want markdown pages. You might want a completely different set of output formats. The right way to use this is to share it with your LLM agent and work together to instantiate a version that fits your needs. The document\'s only job is to communicate the pattern. Your LLM can figure out the rest.\\r\\n---\\r\\ntype: source\\r\\nsubject: Bitcoin from scratch: learning versus production boundaries\\r\\ncreated: 2026-10-08\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-08\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\ntags: [karpathy, source-compilation]\\r\\nsources:\\r\\n  - ../../../../raw/sources/karpathy-brain/raw/blog/md/github-blog/karpathy.github.io_2021_06_21_blockchain.md\\r\\nsemantic-status: compiled-text\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Bitcoin from scratch: learning versus production boundaries\\r\\n\\r\\nAuthor: Andrej Karpathy. Published: 2021-06-21. Captured: 2026-10-08T09:34:58.574395Z.\\r\\nOriginal: [Bitcoin from scratch: learning versus production boundaries](https://karpathy.github.io/2021/06/21/blockchain/). SHA-256: `24574bddd1427a9998c0344645ee4bcd95c82c32f08ac19fa54df3a7b641c647`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What this source says\\r\\n\\r\\nKarpathy reconstructs a legacy P2PKH test-network transaction from Python data structures. The tutorial walks through elliptic-curve identities, modular arithmetic, double-and-add multiplication, handwritten SHA256 and adapted RIPEMD160, compressed keys and checksum addresses, whole-UTXO consumption with change, locking/unlocking scripts, byte-order/variable-length serialization and ECDSA signatures. He reports two broadcast transactions and explains a final consolidation across independently signed inputs. The conclusion distinguishes cryptographic primitives from serialization and compatibility complexity, excludes validation/mining implementation, and says not to roll production cryptography.\\r\\n\\r\\nShort exact evidence from the [archived text](../../../../raw/sources/karpathy-brain/raw/blog/md/github-blog/karpathy.github.io_2021_06_21_blockchain.md):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Please don’t use this anywhere close to anything that touches production.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Interpretation and limits\\r\\n\\r\\nThis independently supports learning by rebuilding an end-to-end mechanism while keeping educational code out of production. The tutorial knowingly uses public reproducible test identities and unsafe signing randomness; those examples are not credentials or acceptable operational implementations. No funds were accessed, transaction broadcast, code run, or historical transaction verified here. Financial, protocol and ecosystem claims remain attributed to 2021; the notebook is a format duplicate, not independent evidence. His quoted understanding maxim is an attribution, not an original aphorism claim. The companion HTML is a format counterpart, not an independent supporting article. Published: Mon, 19 Dec 2016 19:50:08 GMT. Captured: 2026-10-08T09:36:44.693544Z.\\r\\nOriginal: [Yes you should understand backprop](https://karpathy.medium.com/yes-you-should-understand-backprop-e2f06eab496b). This does not claim complete visual or linked-source review.\\r\\n\\r\\n[Archived evidence](../../../../raw/sources/karpathy-brain/raw/blog/md/medium/karpathy.medium.com_yes-you-should-understand-backprop-e2f06eab496b.md). SHA-256: `c038b2c302de83444f5c2afd6a4e648231154202dcb82c91cf7d3de9bc789f4a`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What this source says\\r\\n\\r\\nKarpathy explains why CS231n assignments require manual forward and backward passes despite automatic differentiation frameworks. Saturated sigmoid activations, dead ReLUs, repeated recurrent multiplication and incorrect clipping illustrate how a plausible forward computation can have harmful gradients. He describes finding an implementation that clipped raw Q-error, eliminating gradients outside the clipping interval, and replacing this with a Huber-loss approach. He recommends intuition about the mechanism and implementation exercises rather than relying only on formal derivations.\\r\\n\\r\\nShort exact evidence from the [archived text](../../../../raw/sources/karpathy-brain/raw/blog/md/medium/karpathy.medium.com_yes-you-should-understand-backprop-e2f06eab496b.md):\\r\\n\\r\\n> Backpropagation is a leaky abstraction\\r\\n\\r\\n## Interpretation and limits\\r\\n\\r\\nUnderstand enough of an abstraction to diagnose its failure modes. Teach with a concrete mechanism, then let the learner implement or reproduce it. Code snippets and TensorFlow limitations are historical, not verified current API guidance. Referenced diagrams were not visually inspected. The companion HTML is a format counterpart, not an independent supporting article. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.6 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"b586e0","wall_time_seconds":0.4112956,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2450,"output":"raw/sources/karpathy-brain/raw/blog/md/github-blog/karpathy.github.io_2019_04_25_recipe.md\\r\\n* **get more data**. First, the by far best and preferred way to regularize a model in any practical setting is to add more real training data. It is a very common mistake to spend a lot engineering cycles trying to squeeze juice out of a small dataset when you could instead be collecting more data. As far as I’m aware adding more data is pretty much the only guaranteed way to monotonically improve the performance of a well-configured neural network almost indefinitely. The other would be ensembles (if you can afford them), but that tops out after ~5 models.\\r\\nIn light of the above two facts, I have developed a specific process for myself that I follow when applying a neural net to a new problem, which I will try to describe. You will see that it takes the two principles above very seriously. In particular, it builds from simple to complex and at every step of the way we make concrete hypotheses about what will happen and then either validate them with an experiment or investigate until we find some issue. What we try to prevent very hard is the introduction of a lot of “unverified” complexity at once, which is bound to introduce bugs/misconfigurations that will take forever to find (if ever). If writing your neural net code was like training one, you’d want to use a very small learning rate and guess and then evaluate the full test set after every iteration.\\r\\nOnce you get a qualitative sense it is also a good idea to write some simple code to search/filter/sort by whatever you can think of (e.g. type of label, size of annotations, number of annotations, etc.) and visualize their distributions and the outliers along any axis. The outliers especially almost always uncover some bugs in data quality or preprocessing.\\r\\n* **overfit one batch**. Overfit a single batch of only a few examples (e.g. as little as two). To do so we increase the capacity of our model (e.g. add layers or filters) and verify that we can reach the lowest achievable loss (e.g. zero). I also like to visualize in the same plot both the label and the prediction and ensure that they end up aligning perfectly once we reach the minimum loss. If they do not, there is a bug somewhere and we cannot continue to the next stage.\\r\\n* **complexify only one at a time**. If you have multiple signals to plug into your classifier I would advise that you plug them in one by one and every time ensure that you get a performance boost you’d expect. Don’t throw the kitchen sink at your model at the start. There are other ways of building up complexity - e.g. you can try to plug in smaller images first and make them bigger later, etc.\\r\\nraw/sources/karpathy-brain/raw/blog/md/bearblog/karpathy.bearblog.dev_vibe-coding-menugen.md\\r\\n**Stripe payments**. Next I wanted to add payments so that people can purchase credits. This means another website, another account, more docs, more keys. I select \\"Next.js\\" as the backend, copy paste the very first snippet of code from the \\"getting started\\" docs into my app and... ERROR. I realized later that Stripe gives you JavaScript code when you select Next.js, but my app is built in TypeScript, so every time I pasted a snippet of code it made Cursor unhappy with linter errors, but Claude patched things up ok over time after I told it to \\"fix errors\\" a few times and after I threatened to switch to ChatGPT. Then back in the Stripe dashboard we create a Product, we create a Price, we find the price key (not the product key!), copy paste all the keys around. Around here, I caught Claude using a really bad idea approach to match up a successful Stripe payment to user credits (it tried to match up the email addresses, but the email the user might give in the Stripe checkout may not be the email of the Google account they signed up with, so the user might not actually get the credits that they purchased). I point this out to Claude and it immediately apologizes and rewrites it correctly by passing around unique user ids in the request metadata. It thanks me for pointing out the issue and tells me that it will do it correctly in the future, which I know is just gaslighting. But since our quick test works, only a few more clicks to upgrade the deployment from Development to Production, now re-do a new Product, redo a new Price, re-copy paste all the keys and ids, locally and in the Vercel settings... and then it worked :)\\r\\n**Clerk authentication**. Claude suggested that we use Clerk for authentication, so I went along with it. Signed up for Clerk, configured the project, got my API keys. At this point Claude hallucinated about 1000 lines of code that appeared to be deprecated Clerk APIs. I had to copy paste a lot of the docs back and forth to get things gradually unstuck. Next, so far, Clerk was running in a \\"Development\\" deployment. To move to a \\"Production\\" deployment, there were more hoops to jump through. Clerk demands that you host your app on a custom domain that you own. `menugen.vercel.com` will not work. So I had to purchase the domain name menugen.app. Then I had to wire the domain to my Vercel project. Then I had to change the DNS records. Then I had to pick an OAuth provider, e.g. I went with Google. But to do that was its own [configuration adventure](https://clerk.com/docs/authentication/social-connections/google) . I had to enable an \\"SSO connection\\". I had to go over to Google Cloud Console and create a new project, and add a new OAuth Credential. I had to wait some time for an approval process around here. I then had to go back and forth between the nested settings of all of Vercel, Clerk and Google for a while to wire it up properly. I thought of quitting the project around here, but I felt better when I woke up the next morning.\\r\\nraw/sources/karpathy-brain/raw/blog/md/github-blog/karpathy.github.io_2016_09_07_phd.md\\r\\n**Case study: my thesis**. To make some of this discussion more concrete I wanted to use the example of how my own PhD unfolded. First, fun fact: my entire thesis is based on work I did in the last 1.5 years of my PhD. i.e. it took me quite a long time to wiggle around in the metaproblem space and find a problem that I felt very excited to work on (the other ~2 years I mostly meandered on 3D things (e.g. Kinect Fusion, 3D meshes, point cloud features) and video things). Then at one point in my 3rd year I randomly stopped by Richard Socher’s office on some Saturday at 2am. We had a chat about interesting problems and I realized that some of his work on images and language was in fact getting at something very interesting (of course, the area at the intersection of images and language goes back quite a lot further than Richard as well). I couldn’t quite see all the papers that would follow but it seemed heuristically very promising: it was highly fertile (a lot of unsolved problems, a lot of interesting possibilities on grounding descriptions to images), I felt that it was very cool and important, it was easy to explain, it seemed to be at the boundary of possible (Deep Learning has just started to work), the datasets had just started to become available (Flickr8K had just come out), it fit nicely into Fei-Fei’s interests and even if I were not successful I’d at least get lots of practice with optimizing interesting deep nets that I could reapply elsewhere. I had a strong feeling of a tsunami of checkmarks as everything clicked in place in my mind. I pitched this to Fei-Fei (my adviser) as an area to dive into the next day and, with relief, she enthusiastically approved, encouraged me, and would later go on to steer me within the space (e.g. Fei-Fei insisted that I do image to sentence generation while I was mostly content with ranking.). I’m happy with how things evolved from there. In short, I meandered around for 2 years stuck around the outer loop, finding something to dive into. Once it clicked for me what that was based on several heuristics, I dug in.\\r\\n**Identify the core contribution**. Before you start writing anything it’s important to identify the single core contribution that your paper makes to the field. I would especially highlight the word *single*. A paper is not a random collection of some experiments you ran that you report on. The paper sells a single thing that was not obvious or present before. You have to argue that the thing is important, that it hasn’t been done before, and then you support its merit experimentally in controlled experiments. The entire paper is organized around this core contribution with surgical precision. In particular it doesn’t have any additional fluff and it doesn’t try to pack anything else on a side. As a concrete example, I made a mistake in one of my earlier papers on [video classification](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/karpathy/deepvideo/deepvideo_cvpr2014.pdf) where I tried to pack in two contributions: 1) a set of architectural layouts for video convnets and an unrelated 2) multi-resolution architecture which gave small improvements. I added it because I reasoned first that maybe someone could find it interesting and follow up on it later and second because I thought that contributions in a paper are additive: two contributions are better than one. Unfortunately, this is false and very wrong. The second contribution was minor/dubious and it diluted the paper, it was distracting, and no one cared. I’ve made a similar mistake again in my [CVPR 2014 paper](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/karpathy/deepimagesent/) which presented two separate models: a ranking model and a generation model. Several good in-retrospect arguments could be made that I should have submitted two separate papers; the reason it was one is more historical than rational.\\r\\n"}'}]

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/torch7/i8sJYlgQPeA\\r\\n-- the problem is that you can\'t call :float() on cudnn module, it won\'t convert\\r\\nfunction replaceModules(net, orig_class_name, replacer)\\r\\n  local nodes, container_nodes = net:findModules(orig_class_name)\\r\\n  for i = 1, #nodes do\\r\\n    for j = 1, #(container_nodes[i].modules) do\\r\\n      if container_nodes[i].modules[j] == nodes[i] then\\r\\n        local orig_mod = container_nodes[i].modules[j]\\r\\n        print(\'replacing a cudnn module with nn equivalent...\')\\r\\n        print(orig_mod)\\r\\n        container_nodes[i].modules[j] = replacer(orig_mod)\\r\\n      end\\r\\n    end\\r\\n  end\\r\\nend\\r\\nfunction cudnnNetToCpu(net)\\r\\n  local net_cpu = net:clone():float()\\r\\n  replaceModules(net_cpu, \'cudnn.SpatialConvolution\', \\r\\n    function(orig_mod)\\r\\n      local cpu_mod = nn.SpatialConvolution(orig_mod.nInputPlane, cpu_mod.bias:copy(orig_mod.bias)\\r\\n      cpu_mod.gradWeight = nil -- sanitize for thinner checkpoint\\r\\n      cpu_mod.gradBias = nil -- sanitize for thinner checkpoint\\r\\n      return cpu_mod\\r\\n    end)\\r\\n  replaceModules(net_cpu, \'cudnn.SpatialMaxPooling\', \\r\\n    function(orig_mod)\\r\\n      local cpu_mod = nn.SpatialMaxPooling(orig_mod.kW, orig_mod.kH, orig_mod.dW, orig_mod.dH, \\r\\n                                           orig_mod.padW, orig_mod.padH)\\r\\n      return cpu_mod\\r\\n    end)\\r\\n  replaceModules(net_cpu, \'cudnn.ReLU\', function() return case. but they shouldnt be)\\r\\n    v.lookup_tables = nil\\r\\n    protos[k]:float() -- ship to CPU\\r\\n  else\\r\\n    error(\'error: strange module in protos: \' .. k)\\r\\n  end\\r\\nend\\r\\n\\r\\nlocal savefile = opt.model .. \'_cpu.t7\' -- append \\"cpu.t7\\" to filename\\r\\ntorch.save(savefile, checkpoint)\\r\\nprint(\'saved \' .. return math.abs(x - y) / math.max(math.abs(x) + math.abs(y), h)\\r\\n  end\\r\\nend\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction gradcheck.numeric_gradient(f, x, df, eps)\\r\\n  df = df or 1.0\\r\\n  eps = eps or 1e-8\\r\\n  local n = x:nElement()\\r\\n  local x_flat = x:view(n)\\r\\n  local dx_num = x.new(#x):zero()\\r\\n  local dx_num_flat = dx_num:view(n)\\r\\n  for i = 1, n do\\r\\n    local orig = eps\\r\\n    local neg = f(x)\\r\\n    if torch.isTensor(df) then\\r\\n      neg = neg:clone()\\r\\n    end\\r\\n    \\r\\n    local d = nil\\r\\n    if torch.isTensor(df) then\\r\\n      d = torch.dot(pos - neg, df) / (2 * eps)\\r\\n    else\\r\\n      d = df * (pos - neg) / (2 * eps)\\r\\n    end\\r\\n    \\r\\n    dx_num_flat[i] = d\\r\\n    x_flat[i] = orig\\r\\n  end\\r\\n  return dx_num\\r\\nend\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n--[[\\r\\nInputs:\\r\\n- f is a function that takes a tensor and returns a scalar\\r\\n- x is the point at which to evalute f\\r\\n- dx is the analytic gradient of f at x\\r\\n--]]\\r\\nfunction gradcheck.check_random_dims(f, x, dx, eps, num_iterations, verbose)\\r\\n  if verbose == nil then verbose = false end\\r\\n  eps = eps or 1e-4\\r\\n\\r\\n  local x_flat = x:view(-1)\\r\\n  local dx_flat = dx:view(-1)\\r\\n\\r\\n  local relative_errors = torch.Tensor(num_iterations)\\r\\n\\r\\n  for t = 1, num_iterations do\\r\\n    -- Make sure the index is really
