(number of synapses per neuron)\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction Brain()\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \\r\\n  //1D array of neuron activations\\r\\n  this.act= new Array(brainsize);\\r\\n  for (var i=0;i<brainsize;i++) {\\r\\n    this.act[i]= 0;\\r\\n  }\\r\\n  \\r\\n  //2D array of synapse weights and indexes of neurons they connect to\\r\\n  this.w= new Array(brainsize);\\r\\n  this.ix= new Array(brainsize);\\r\\n  for (var i=0;i<brainsize;i++) {\\r\\n    this.w[i]= new Array(braindensity);\\r\\n    this.ix[i]= new Array(braindensity);\\r\\n    for (var j=0;j<braindensity;j++) {\\r\\n        this.w[i][j]= randf(-1.2, 1.2);\\r\\n        this.ix[i][j]= randi(0, brainsize);\\r\\n    }\\r\\n  }\\r\\n  \\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n//feeds forward the brain. s1 and s2 are the two senses, both in [0,1]\\r\\n//health is ... health\\r\\nBrain.prototype = {\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //brain takes inputs and sets its outputs\\r\\n    tick : function(s1, s2) {\\r\\n\\r\\n        this.act[0]= s1; //set inputs\\r\\n        this.act[1]= s2;\\r\\n        this.act[3]= 1; //some bias neurons are always on\\r\\n        this.act[4]= 1;\\r\\n        this.act[5]= 1;\\r\\n        this.act[6]= 1;\\r\\n        \\r\\n        for (var i=7;i<brainsize;i++) {\\r\\n            var a=0;\\r\\n            for (var j=0;j<braindensity;j++) {\\r\\n                a+= this.w[i][j]*this.act[this.ix[i][j]]\\r\\n            }\\r\\n            this.act[i]= 1.0/(1.0 + Math.exp(-a));  //pass through sigmoid\\r\\n        }\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //assume last 2 neurons are the outputs\\r\\n        return {\\r\\n            out0: this.act[brainsize-1] - 0.5, \\r\\n            out1: this.act[brainsize-2]\\r\\n        };\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //used during reproduction\\r\\n    //copy over the brain with some mutation. crude. for now\\r\\n    mutateFrom : function(brain) {\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //lossy copy of brain structure\\r\\n        for (var i=0;i<brainsize;i++) {\\r\\n          for (var j=0;j<braindensity;j++) {\\r\\n            \\r\\n            var m= brain.w[i][j];\\r\\n            if(randf(0,1)<mutrate) m += randn(0,mutrate2);\\r\\n            this.w[i][j]= m;\\r\\n            \\r\\n            m= brain.ix[i][j];\\r\\n            if(randf(0,1)<mutrate) m = randi(0,brainsize);\\r\\n            this.ix[i][j]= m;\\r\\n          }\\r\\n        }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction Agent(){\\r\\n    this.pos= new Vector2D(randf(0,WIDTH), randf(0,HEIGHT));\\r\\n    this.dir= randf(0, 2*Math.PI);\\r\\n    this.s1= 0;  //food sense eye 1\\r\\n    this.s2= 0;  //food sense eye 2\\r\\n    this.brain= new Brain();\\r\\n    this.speed= 4.0;\\r\\n    this.boost= 0.0; //boost, on top of speed\\r\\n    this.health= 1.0;\\r\\n    this.rep= 0.0; //replication counter\\r\\n    this.selected= false;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction myinit(){\\r\\n    counter = 0;\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //cosmetics\\r\\n    ctx.font = \\"12pt Arial\\";\\r\\n    ctx.strokeStyle=\\"black\\";\\r\\n    ctx.lineWidth=\\"1.5\\";\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction update(){\\r\\n    counter=counter+1;\\r\\n    \\r\\n    killi=-1;\\r\\n    for(i in agents) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[i];\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //move agent\\r\\n        var vel= new Vector2D((a.boost+a.speed)*Math.cos(a.dir), (a.boost+a.speed)*Math.sin(a.dir));\\r\\n        a.pos.plusEq(vel);\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //enforce boundary conditions: wrap around if necessary\\r\\n        if(a.pos.x<0) a.pos.x= WIDTH;\\r\\n        if(a.pos.x>WIDTH) a.pos.x= 0;\\r\\n        if(a.pos.y<0) a.pos.y= HEIGHT;\\r\\n        if(a.pos.y>HEIGHT) a.pos.y= 0;\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //agent gets more hungry\\r\\n        a.health-= foodloss;\\r\\n        a.health-= boostcost*a.boost; //boost costs health\\r\\n        if(a.health<0) { killi= i; }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    if(killi!=-1) agents.splice(killi, 1);\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //agent collision detection and resolution\\r\\n    for(i in agents) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[i];\\r\\n        for(j in agents) {\\r\\n            var a2 = agents[j];\\r\\n            if(i==j) continue;\\r\\n            var d= Math.sqrt(Math.pow(a.pos.x-a2.pos.x,2) + Math.pow(a.pos.y-a2.pos.y,2));\\r\\n            var overlap= rad*2-d;\\r\\n            if(overlap>0 && d>1){\\r\\n                //one agent pushes on another proportional to his boost. a.s2=0;\\r\\n        \\r\\n        for(j in food) {\\r\\n            var f = food[j];\\r\\n            \\r\\n            var d2= Math.sqrt(Math.pow(a.pos.x-f.pos.x,2) + Math.pow(a.pos.y-f.pos.y,2));\\r\\n            if(d2 < rad){\\r\\n                a.rep+= foodgain;\\r\\n                a.health+= foodgain;\\r\\n                if(a.health>1) a.health= 1;\\r\\n                killi= j;\\r\\n            }\\r\\n            \\r\\n            if(d2 < rad*10) { //for efficiency, don\'t even bother if it\'s too far\\r\\n                \\r\\n                //compute position of both eyes in world coordinates\\r\\n                var x1= a.pos.x + eyelen*Math.cos(a.dir - eyesep);\\r\\n                var y1= a.pos.y + eyelen*Math.sin(a.dir - eyesep);\\r\\n                var x2= a.pos.x + eyelen*Math.cos(a.dir + eyesep);\\r\\n                var y2= a.pos.y + eyelen*Math.sin(a.dir + eyesep);\\r\\n                \\r\\n                a.s1 += eyemult*Math.exp(-eyesens*(Math.pow(x1-f.pos.x,2) + Math.pow(y1-f.pos.y,2)));\\r\\n                a.s2 += eyemult*Math.exp(-eyesens*(Math.pow(x2-f.pos.x,2) + Math.pow(y2-f.pos.y,2)));\\r\\n            }\\r\\n        }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    if(killi!=-1) food.splice(killi, 1);\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //feed forward the brain from senses to output\\r\\n    for(i in agents) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[i];\\r\\n        res= a.brain.tick(a.s1, a.s2);\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //apply output neuron 0: controls turning. Also cap it to a max of 0.3 rotation\\r\\n        var des= res.out0;\\r\\n        if(des>0.8)des=0.8;\\r\\n        if(des<-0.8)des=-0.8;\\r\\n        a.dir += des;\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //wrap direction around to keep it in range of [0, 2pi]\\r\\n        if(a.dir>2*Math.PI) a.dir= a.dir-2*Math.PI;\\r\\n        if(a.dir<0)a.dir=2*Math.PI+a.dir;\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //apply output neuron 1: controls boost\\r\\n        des= res.out1;\\r\\n        if(des>0) {a.boost= des;}\\r\\n        else {a.boost= 0;}\\r\\n     }\\r\\n     \\r\\n    //spawn more food, maybe\\r\\n    if(counter%foodaddfreq==0 && food.length<foodlimit) {\\r\\n        var f = {\\r\\n            pos: new Vector2D(randf(0,WIDTH), randf(0,HEIGHT))\\r\\n        };\\r\\n        food.push(f);\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //handle births\\r\\n    var bi= -1;\\r\\n    for(i in agents) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[i];\\r\\n        if(a.rep>repthr) {\\r\\n            //this agent reproduces!\\r\\n            bi= i;\\r\\n        }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    \\r\\n    if(bi!=-1) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[bi];\\r\\n        a.rep= 0;\\r\\n        \\r\\n         var anew= new Agent();\\r\\n         anew.pos=  new Vector2D(a.pos.x + randf(-30,30), a.pos.y + randf(-30,30));\\r\\n         anew.brain.mutateFrom(a.brain);\\r\\n        \\r\\n        agents.push(anew);\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //spawn more agents if there are too few agents left\\r\\n    if(agents.length<10) {\\r\\n        var anew= new Agent();\\r\\n        agents.push(anew);\\r\\n    }\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction draw(){\\r\\n    ctx.clearRect(0,0,WIDTH,HEIGHT);\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //draw food\\r\\n    ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(100,230,100)\';\\r\\n    for(i in food) {\\r\\n        var f = food[i];\\r\\n        drawCircle(f.pos.x, f.pos.y, 10);\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //draw all agents\\r\\n    for(i in agents) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[i];\\r\\n        \\r\\n        ctx.save();\\r\\n        ctx.translate(a.pos.x, a.pos.y);\\r\\n        ctx.rotate(a.dir - Math.PI/2);\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //draw its eyes\\r\\n        //first compute their position\\r\\n        var a1= -eyesep + Math.PI/2;\\r\\n        var a2= eyesep + Math.PI/2;\\r\\n        var x1= Math.cos(a1)*eyelen; var y1= Math.sin(a1)*eyelen;\\r\\n        var x2= Math.cos(a2)*eyelen; var y2= Math.sin(a2)*eyelen;\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //draw the lines to eyes\\r\\n        ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(0,0,0)\';\\r\\n        ctx.beginPath();\\r\\n        ctx.moveTo(0, 0);\\r\\n        ctx.lineTo(x1, y1);\\r\\n        ctx.moveTo(0, 0);\\r\\n        ctx.lineTo(x2, y2);\\r\\n        ctx.closePath();\\r\\n        ctx.stroke();\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //draw the eyes, colored by how much food they sense\\r\\n        var s= Math.round(a.s1*255.0);\\r\\n        ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(\'+s+\',0,0)\';\\r\\n        drawCircle(x1, y1, 5)\\r\\n        var s= Math.round(a.s2*255.0); if(s>255) s=255;\\r\\n        ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(\'+s+\',0,0)\';\\r\\n        drawCircle(x2, y2, 5)\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //draw agent body and outline\\r\\n        if (!a.selected){\\r\\n            ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(0,\'+Math.round(255.0*a.health)+\',\'+Math.round(255.0*a.health)+\')\';\\r\\n        }\\r\\n        drawCircle(0, 0, rad);\\r\\n        ctx.restore();\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //draw brain of this agent, if it is selected\\r\\n        if(a.selected) {\\r\\n            \\r\\n            //draw all the connections first\\r\\n            ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(0,0,0)\';\\r\\n            ctx.beginPath();\\r\\n            var SS=100;\\r\\n            for (var m=0;m<brainsize;m++) {\\r\\n                var r1= 2*Math.PI*m/brainsize;\\r\\n                for (var n=0;n<braindensity;n++) {\\r\\n                    //this.w[i][j]*this.act[this.ix[i][j]]\\r\\n                    var act= Math.round(a.brain.w[i][j]*120+120);\\r\\n                    var r2= ctx.lineTo(SS*Math.cos(r2)+WIDTH-SS*1.5, SS*Math.sin(r2)+HEIGHT-SS*1.5);\\r\\n                }\\r\\n            }\\r\\n            ctx.stroke();\\r\\n            \\r\\n            for (var m=0;m<brainsize;m++) {\\r\\n                //var act= 1.0/(1.0 + Math.exp(-a));  //pass through sigmoid\\r\\n                var act= Math.round(a.brain.act[m]*255);\\r\\n d= Math.sqrt(Math.pow(a.pos.x-x,2) + Math.pow(a.pos.y-y,2));\\r\\n        if(d<3*rad) {\\r\\n        \\r\\n            //that\'s a hit! Let\'s select this one and unselect all others\\r\\n            var newset= !a.selected;\\r\\n            var j;\\r\\n            for(j in agents) { agents[j].selected= false; }\\r\\n            a.selected= newset;\\r\\n            \\r\\n            return;\\r\\n        }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction keyUp(key){\\r\\n}\\r\\nfunction keyDown(key){\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n</script>\\r\\n\\r\\n<style type=\\"text/css\\">\\r\\ncanvas { \\r\\n    border: 1px solid #555;\\r\\n    margin-top: 20px;\\r\\n}\\r\\nh1 {\\r\\n    font-weight: normal;\\r\\n    padding: 0;\\r\\n    margin: 0;\\r\\n}\\r\\nh2 {\\r\\n    font-weight: normal;\\r\\n    font-size: 12px;\\r\\n    \\r\\n}\\r\\nbody {\\r\\n    text-align: center;\\r\\n    font-family: Verdana, Helvetica, sans-serif;\\r\\n    font-size: 12px;\\r\\n}\\r\\n.ex{\\r\\n    width: 500px;\\r\\n    margin-left: auto;\\r\\n    margin-right: auto;\\r\\n}\\r\\n</style>\\r\\n\\r\\n</head>\\r\\n<body onLoad=\\"NPGinit(50);\\">\\r\\n<h1>Canvas Artifical Life evolutionary simulation v0.1</h1>\\r\\n<h2>by <a href=\\"http://twitter.com/#!/karpathy\\" target=\\"_blank\\">@karpathy</a><h2/>\\r\\n<p>Click on a bot to select it and see its neural network activations.</p>\\r\\n<canvas id=\\"NPGcanvas\\" width=\\"800\\" height=\\"600\\">Browser not suppoerted for Canvas. repos/karpathy/notpygamejs/demos/exgame.html\\r\\n<html>\\r\\n<head>\\r\\n<title>Canvas game</title>\\r\\n\\r\\n<script src=\\"../include/npgmain.js\\"></script>\\r\\n<script type=\\"text/javascript\\">\\r\\n\\r\\nvar agents = new Array();\\r\\nvar selected = 0;\\r\\nvar bubbleLife = 0; var bubblex = 0; var bubbley = 0; var bubblem = 0; var bubblei = 0;\\r\\nvar desiredx = 0; var desiredy = 0;\\r\\nvar score = 0;\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction myinit(){\\r\\n    for(i = 0; i<5; i++) { \\r\\n        var a = {\\r\\n                xpos:WIDTH*Math.random(), \\r\\n                ypos:HEIGHT*Math.random(), \\r\\n                xtarget:WIDTH*Math.random(), \\r\\n                ytarget:HEIGHT*Math.random(), \\r\\n                speed:3, \\r\\n                rad:20\\r\\n                };\\r\\n        agents.push(a);\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    ctx.font = \\"14pt Arial\\";\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction update(){\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //move every agent towards his target\\r\\n    for(i in agents) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[i];\\r\\n        var xoff = a.xtarget-a.xpos;\\r\\n        var yoff = a.ytarget-a.ypos;\\r\\n        var d = Math.sqrt(xoff*xoff + yoff*yoff);\\r\\n        xoff = a.speed*xoff/d;\\r\\n        yoff = a.speed*yoff/d;\\r\\n        if (d>a.speed) {\\r\\n            a.xpos = a.xpos + xoff;\\r\\n            a.ypos = a.ypos + yoff;\\r\\n        }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //handle game \\"dynamics\\"\\r\\n    if(bubbleLife>0) bubbleLife--;\\r\\n    if(bubbleLife<=0 && Math.random()<0.01){\\r\\n    \\r\\n        //instatiate new request\\r\\n        var ri = Math.floor(Math.random()*agents.length)\\r\\n        bubblex = agents[ri].xpos;\\r\\n        bubbley = agents[ri].ypos + 30;\\r\\n        bubbleLife = 130 + Math.floor(Math.random()*60);\\r\\n        bubblem = Math.floor(Math.random()*3);\\r\\n        bubblei = ri;\\r\\n        desiredx = Math.random()*WIDTH;\\r\\n        desiredy = Math.random()*HEIGHT;\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    \\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction draw(){\\r\\n    ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(255,255,255)\';\\r\\n    ctx.fillRect(0,0,WIDTH,HEIGHT);\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //draw bubble, if applicable, and desired location\\r\\n    if(bubbleLife>0) {\\r\\n        drawBubble(bubblex, bubbley, 230, 50, 20);\\r\\n        ctx.fillStyle = \'rgb(0,0,0)\';\\r\\n        \\r\\n        if(bubblem==0) ctx.fillText(\\"Move me!!! Move me!!!\\", bubblex+20, bubbley+30); \\r\\n        else if(bubblem==1) ctx.fillText(\\"PLEASE MOVE ME!\\", bubblex+20, bubbley+30); \\r\\n        else ctx.fillText(\\"MOVE MEEEEEeeee\\", bubblex+20, bubbley+30); \\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction mouseClick(x, y){\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //select an agent if we clicked on one\\r\\n    var agentSelected = 0;\\r\\n    for(i in agents) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[i];\\r\\n        var xoff = x-a.xpos;\\r\\n        var yoff = y-a.ypos;\\r\\n        var d = Math.sqrt(xoff*xoff + yoff*yoff);\\r\\n        if (d<a.rad && i!=selected) {\\r\\n            selected = i;\\r\\n            agentSelected = 1;\\r\\n        }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    \\r\\n    //otherwise send the selected agent somewhere\\r\\n    if(agentSelected==0 && selected!=-1) {\\r\\n        var a = agents[selected];\\r\\n        a.xtarget = x;\\r\\n        a.ytarget = y;\\r\\n        \\r\\n        //find distance to desired location\\r\\n        var xoff = x-desiredx;\\r\\n        var yoff = y-desiredy;\\r\\n        var d = Math.sqrt(xoff*xoff + yoff*yoff);\\r\\n        \\r\\n        if (bubblei == selected && d < 30) {\\r\\n            score += bubbleLife;\\r\\n            bubbleLife = 0;\\r\\n        }\\r\\n    }\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n</script>\\r\\n\\r\\n<style type=\\"text/css\\">\\r\\ncanvas { \\r\\n    border: 1px solid #555;\\r\\n    margin-top: 100px;\\r\\n}\\r\\nbody {\\r\\n    text-align: center;\\r\\n    font-family: Verdana, Helvetica, sans-serif;\\r\\n    font-size: 12px;\\r\\n}\\r\\n</style>\\r\\n\\r\\n</head>\\r\\n<body onLoad=\\"NPGinit(50);\\">\\r\\n<canvas id=\\"NPGcanvas\\" width=\\"500\\" height=\\"500\\">Browser not suppoerted for Canvas. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.8 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Warning: truncated output (original token count: 10718)\nTotal output lines: 1\n\n{"chunk_id":"0b6e6d","wall_time_seconds":0.6222561,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":10387,"output":"\\r\\nFILE 56 repos/karpathy/paper-notes/matching_networks.md\\r\\n# Matching Networks for One Shot Learning\\r\\n\\r\\nBy DeepMind crew: **Oriol Vinyals, Charles Blundell, Timothy Lillicrap, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Daan Wierstra**\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is a paper on **one-shot** learning, where we\'d like to learn a class based on very few (or indeed, 1) training examples. E.g. it suffices to show a child a single giraffe, not a few hundred thousands before it can recognize more giraffes.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis paper falls into a category of *\\"duh of course\\"* kind of paper, something very interesting, powerful, but somehow obvious only in retrospect. I like it.\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose you\'re given a single example of some class and would like to label it in test images.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Observation 1**: a standard approach might be to train an Exemplar SVM for this one (or few) examples vs. all the other training examples - i.e. a linear classifier. But this requires optimization.\\r\\n- **Observation 2:** known non-parameteric alternatives (e.g. k-Nearest Neighbor) don\'t suffer from this problem. E.g. I could immediately use a Nearest Neighbor to classify the new class without having to do any optimization whatsoever. However, NN is gross because it depends on an (arbitrarily-chosen) metric, e.g. L2 distance. Ew.\\r\\n- **Core idea**: lets train a fully end-to-end nearest neighbor classifer!![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 10.08.44 PM](/img/matching_networks/Screen%20Shot%202016-08-07%20at%2010.08.44%20PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The training protocol\\r\\n\\r\\nAs the authors amusingly point out in the conclusion (and this is the *duh of course* part), *\\"one-shot learning is much easier if you train the network to do one-shot learning\\"*. Therefore, we want the test-time protocol (given N novel classes with only k examples each (e.g. k = 1 or 5), predict new instances to one of N classes) to exactly match the training time protocol.\\r\\n\\r\\nTo create each \\"episode\\" of training from a dataset of examples then:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Sample a task T from the training data, e.g. select 5 labels, and up to 5 examples per label (i.e. 5-25 examples).\\r\\n2. To form one episode sample a label set L (e.g. {cats, dogs}) and then use L to sample the support set S and a batch B of examples to evaluate loss on.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe idea on high level is clear but the writing here is a bit unclear on details, of exactly how the sampling is done.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The model\\r\\n\\r\\nI find the paper\'s model description slightly wordy and unclear, but basically we\'re building a **differentiable nearest neighbor++**. The output \\\\hat{y} for a test example \\\\hat{x} is computed very similar to what you might see in Nearest Neighbors:![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 11.14.26 PM](img/matching_networks/Screen%20Shot%202016-08-07%20at%2011.14.26%20PM.png)\\r\\nwhere **a** acts as a kernel, computing the extent to which \\\\hat{x} is similar to a training example x_i, and then the labels from the training examples (y_i) are weight-blended together accordingly. The paper doesn\'t mention this but I assume for classification y_i would presumbly be one-hot vectors.\\r\\n\\r\\nNow, we\'re going to embed both the training examples x_i and the test example \\\\hat{x}, and we\'ll interpret their inner products (or here a cosine similarity) as the \\"match\\", and pass that through a softmax to get normalized mixing weights so they add up to 1. No surprises here, this is quite natural:\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 11.20.29 PM](img/matching_networks/Screen%20Shot%202016-08-07%20at%2011.20.29%20PM.png)\\r\\nHere **c()** is cosine distance, which I presume is implemented by normalizing the two input vectors to have unit L2 norm and taking a dot product. I assume the authors tried skipping the normalization too and it did worse? Anyway, now all that\'s left to define is the function **f** (i.e. how do we embed the test example into a vector) and the function **g** (i.e. how do we embed each training example into a vector?).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Embedding the training examples.** This (the function **g**) is a bidirectional LSTM over the examples:\\r\\n\\r\\n ![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 11.57.10 PM](img/matching_networks/Screen%20Shot%202016-08-07%20at%2011.57.10%20PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\ni.e. encoding of i\'th example x_i is a function of its \\"raw\\" embedding g\'(x_i) and the embedding of its friends, communicated through the bidirectional network\'s hidden states. i.e. each training example is a function of not just itself but all of its friends in the set. This is part of the ++ above, because in a normal nearest neighbor you wouldn\'t change the representation of an example as a function of the other data points in the training set.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt\'s odd that the **order** is not mentioned, I assume it\'s random? This is a bit gross because order matters to a bidirectional LSTM; you\'d get different embeddings if you permute the examples. \\r\\n\\r\\n**Embedding the test example.** This (the function **f**) is a an LSTM that processes for a fixed amount (K time steps) and at each point also *attends* over the examples in the training set. The encoding is the last hidden state of the LSTM. Again, this way we\'re allowing the network to change its encoding of the test example as a function of the training examples. Nifty: ![Screen Shot 2016-08-08 at 12.11.15 AM](img/matching_networks/Screen%20Shot%202016-08-08%20at%2012.11.15%20AM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nThat looks scary at first but it\'s really just a vanilla LSTM with attention where the input at each time step is constant (f\'(\\\\hat{x}), an encoding of the test example all by itself) and the hidden state is a function of previous hidden state but also a concatenated readout vector **r**, which we obtain by attending over the encoded training examples (encoded with **g** from above).\\r\\n\\r\\nOh and I assume there is a typo in equation (5), it should say r_k = … without the -1 on LHS. \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Experiments\\r\\n\\r\\n**Task**: N-way k-shot learning task. i.e. we\'re given k (e.g. 1 or 5) labelled examples for N classes that we have not previously trained on and asked to classify new instances into he N classes.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Baselines:** an \\"obvious\\" strategy of using a pretrained ConvNet and doing nearest neighbor based on the codes. An option of finetuning the network on the new examples as well (requires training and careful and strong regularization!).\\r\\n\\r\\n**MANN** of Santoro et al. [21]: Also a DeepMind paper, a fun NTM-like Meta-Learning approach that is fed a sequence of examples and asked to predict their labels.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Siamese network** of Koch et al. [11]: A siamese network that takes two examples and predicts whether they are from the same class or not with logistic regression. A test example is labeled with a nearest neighbor: with the class it matches best according to the siamese net (requires iteration over all training examples one by one). Also, this approach is less end-to-end than the one here because it requires the ad-hoc nearest neighbor matching, while here the *exact* end task is optimized for. It\'s beautiful.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### Omniglot experiments \\r\\n\\r\\n### ![Screen Shot 2016-08-08 at 10.21.45 AM](img/matching_networks/Screen%20Shot%202016-08-08%20at%2010.21.45%20AM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nOmniglot of [Lake et al. [14]](http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~rsalakhu/papers/LakeEtAl2015Science.pdf) is a MNIST-like scribbles dataset with 1623 characters with 20 examples each.\\r\\n\\r\\nImage encoder is a CNN with 4 modules of [3x3 CONV 64 filters, batchnorm, ReLU, 2x2 max pool]. The original image is claimed to be so resized from original 28x28 to 1x1x64, which doesn\'t make sense because factor of 2 downsampling 4 times is reduction of 16, and 28/16 is a non-integer >1. I\'m assuming they use VALID convs?\\r\\n\\r\\nResults: ![Screen Shot 2016-08-08 at 10.27.46 AM](img/matching_networks/Screen%20Shot%202016-08-08%20at%2010.27.46%20AM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nMatching nets do best. Fully Conditional Embeddings (FCE) by which I mean they the \\"Full Context Embeddings\\" of Section 2.1.2 instead are not used here, mentioned to not work much better. Finetuning helps a bit on baselines but not with Matching nets (weird).\\r\\n\\r\\nThe comparisons in this table are somewhat confusing:\\r\\n\\r\\n- I can\'t find the MANN numbers of 82.8% and 94.9% in their paper [21]; not clear where they come from. E.g. for 5 classes and 5-shot they seem to report 88.4% not 94.9% as seen here. I must be missing something.\\r\\n- I also can\'t find the numbers reported here in the Siamese Net [11] paper. As far as I can tell in their Table 2 they report one-shot accuracy, 20-way classification to be 92.0, while here it is listed as 88.1%?\\r\\n- The results of Lake et al. [14] who proposed Omniglot are also missing from the table. If I\'m understanding this correctly they report 95.2% on 1-shot 20-way, while matching nets here show 93.8%, and humans are estimated at 95.5%. That is, the results here appear weaker than those of Lake et al., but one should keep in mind that the method here is significantly more generic and does not make any assumptions about the existence of strokes, etc., and it\'s a simple, single fully-differentiable blob of neural stuff.\\r\\n\\r\\n(skipping ImageNet/LM experiments as there are few surprises)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Conclusions\\r\\n\\r\\nGood paper, effectively develops a differentiable nearest neighbor trained end-to-end. It\'s something new, I like it!\\r\\n\\r\\nA few concerns: \\r\\n\\r\\n- A bidirectional LSTMs (not order-invariant compute) is applied over sets of training examples to encode them. The authors don\'t talk about the order actually used, which presumably is random, or mention this potentially unsatisfying feature. This can be solved by using a recurrent attentional mechanism instead, as the authors are certainly aware of and as has been discussed at length in [ORDER MATTERS: SEQUENCE TO SEQUENCE FOR SETS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06391), where Oriol is also the first author. I wish there was a comment on this point in the paper somewhere.\\r\\n\\r\\n- The approach also gets quite a bit slower as the number of training examples grow, but once this number is large one would presumable switch over to a parameteric approach.\\r\\n\\r\\n- It\'s also potentially concerning that during training the method uses a specific number of examples, e.g. 5-25, so this is the number of that must also be used at test time. What happens if we want the size of our training set to grow online? It appears that we need to retrain the network because the encoder LSTM for the training data is not \\"used to\\" seeing inputs of more examples? That is unless you fall back to iteratively subsampling the training data, doing multiple inference passes and averaging, or something like that. If we don\'t use FCE it can still be that the attention mechanism LSTM can still not be \\"used to\\" attending over many more examples, but it\'s not clear how much this matters. An interesting experiment would be to not use FCE and try to use 100 or 1000 training examples, while only training on up to 25 (with and fithout FCE). Discussion surrounding this point would be interesting.\\r\\n\\r\\n- Not clear what happened with the Omniglot experiments, with incorrect numbers for [11], [21], and the exclusion of Lake et al. [14] comparison.\\r\\n\\r\\n- A baseline that is missing would in my opinion also include training of an [Exemplar SVM](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~tmalisie/projects/iccv11/), which is a much more powerful approach than encode-with-a-cnn-and-nearest-neighbor.\\r\\n\\r\\n  \u200b\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE 57 repos/karpathy/paper-notes/vin.md\\r\\n# Value Iteration Networks\\r\\n\\r\\n**By Berkeley group: Aviv Tamar, Yi Wu, Garrett Thomas, Sergey Levine, and Pieter Abbeel**\\r\\n\\r\\n[Paper link](http://arxiv.org/abs/1602.02867).\\r\\n\\r\\nThis paper introduces a policy network architecture for RL tasks that has an embedded differentiable *planning module*, trained end-to-end. It hence falls into a category of fun papers that take explicit algorithms, make them differentiable, embed them in a larger neural net, and train everything end-to-end.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Observation**: in most RL approaches the policy is a \\"reactive\\" controller that internalizes into its weights actions that historically led to high rewards.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Insight**: To improve the inductive bias of the model, embed a specifically-structured neural net planner into the policy. In particular, the planner runs the value Iteration algorithm, which can be implemented with a ConvNet. So this is kind of like a model-based approach trained with model-free RL, or something. Lol.\\r\\n\\r\\nNOTE: This is very different from the more standard/obvious approach of learning a separate neural network environment dynamics model (e.g. with regression), fixing it, and then using a planning algorithm over this intermediate representation. This would not be end-to-end because we\'re not backpropagating the end objective through the full model but rely on auxiliary objectives (e.g. log prob of a state given previous state and action when training a dynamics model), and in practice also does not work well.\\r\\n\\r\\nNOTE2: A recurrent agent (e.g. with an LSTM policy), or a feedforward agent with a sufficiently deep network trained in a model-free setting has some capacity to learn planning-like computation in its hidden states. However, this is nowhere near as explicit as in this paper, since here we\'re directly \\"baking\\" the planning compute into the architecture. It\'s exciting.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Value Iteration\\r\\n\\r\\nValue Iteration is an algorithm for computing the optimal value function/policy $V^*, \\\\pi^*$ and involves turning the Bellman equation into a recurrence:\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM.png)\\r\\nThis iteration converges to $V^*$ as $n \\\\rightarrow \\\\infty$, which we can use to behave optimally (i.e. the optimal policy takes actions that lead to the most rewarding states, according to $V^*$). \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Grid-world domain\\r\\n\\r\\nThe paper ends up running the model on several domains, but for the sake of an effective example consider the grid-world task where the agent is at some particular position in a 2D grid and has to reach a specific goal state while also avoiding obstacles. Here is an example of the toy task:\\r\\n\\r\\n ![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.43.04 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.43.04 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe agent gets a reward +1 in the goal state, -1 in obstacles (black), and -0.01 for each step (so that the shortest path to the goal is an optimal solution).\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## VIN model\\r\\n\\r\\nThe agent is implemented in a very straight-forward manner as a single neural network trained with TRPO (Policy Gradients with a KL constraint on predictive action distributions over a batch of trajectories). So the only loss function used is to maximize expected reward, as is standard in model-free RL. However, the policy network of the agent has a very specific structure since it (internally) runs value iteration.\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst, there\'s the core Value Iteration **(VI) Module** which runs the recurrence formula (reproducing again):\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM.png)\\r\\nThe input to this recurrence are the two arrays R (the reward array, reward for each state) and P (the dynamics array, the probabilities of transitioning to nearby states with each action), which are of course unknown to the agent, but can be predicted with neural networks as a function of the current state. This is a little funny because the networks take a _particular_ state **s** and are internally (during the forward pass) predicting the rewards and dynamics for all states and actions in the entire environment. Notice, extremely importantly and once again, that at no point are the reward and dynamics functions explicitly regressed to the observed transitions in the environment. They are just arrays of numbers that plug into value iteration recurrence module.\\r\\n\\r\\nBut anyway, once we have **R,P** arrays, in the Grid-world above due to the local connectivity, value iteration can be implemented with a repeated application of convolving **P** over **R**, as these filters effectively *diffuse* the estimated reward function (**R**) through the dynamics model (**P**), followed by max pooling across the actions. If **P** is a not a function of the state, it would simply be the filters in the Conv layer. Notice that posing this as convolution also assumes that the env dynamics are position-invariant. See the diagram below on the right:![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.58.42 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.58.42 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nOnce the array of numbers that we interpret as holding the estimated $V^*$ is computed after running **K** steps of the recurrence (K is fixed beforehand. For example for a 16x16 map it is 20, since that\'s a bit more than the amount of steps needed to diffuse rewards across the entire map), we \\"pluck out\\" the state-action values $Q(s,.)$ at the state the agent happens to currently be in (by an \\"attention\\" operator $\\\\psi$), and (optionally) append these Q values to the feedforward representation of the current state $\\\\phi(s)$, and finally predicting the action distribution.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Experiments\\r\\n\\r\\n**Baseline 1**: A vanilla ConvNet policy trained with TRPO. [(50 3x3 filters)\\\\*2, 2x2 max pool, (100 3x3 filters)\\\\*3, 2x2 max pool, FC(100), FC(4), Softmax].\\r\\n\\r\\n**Baseline 2**: A fully convolutional network (FCN), 3 layers (with a filter that spans the whole image), of 150, 100, 10 filters. i.e. slightly different and perhaps a bit more domain-appropriate ConvNet architecture.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Curriculum** is used during training where easier environments are trained on first. This is claimed to work better but not quantified in tables. Models are trained with TRPO, RMSProp, implemented in Theano.\\r\\n\\r\\nResults when training on **5000** random grid-world instances (hey isn\'t that quite a bit low?):![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 5.47.23 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 5.47.23 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nTLDR VIN generalizes better.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe authors also run the model on the **Mars Rover Navigation** dataset (wait what?), a **Continuous Control** 2D path planning dataset, and the **WebNav Challenge**, a language-based search task on a graph (of a subset of Wikipedia). Skipping these because they don\'t add _too_ much to the core cool idea of the paper.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Misc\\r\\n\\r\\n**The good**: I really like this paper because the core idea is cute (the planner is *embedded* in the policy and trained end-to-end), novel (I don\'t think I saw this idea executed on so far elsewhere), the paper is well-written and clear, and the supplementary materials are thorough.\\r\\n\\r\\n**On the approach**: Significant challenges remain to make this approach more practically viable, but it also seems that much more exciting followup work can be done in this framework. I wish the authors discussed this more in the conclusion. In particular, it seems that one has to explicitly encode the environment connectivity structure in the internal model $\\\\bar{M}$. How much of a problem is this and what could be done about it? Or how could we do the planning in more higher-level abstract spaces instead of the actual low-level state space of the problem? Also, it seems that a potentially nice feature of this approach is that the agent could dynamically \\"decide\\" on a reward function at runtime, and the VI module can diffuse it through the dynamics and hence do the planning.  A potentially interesting outcome is that the agent could utilize this kind of computation so that  an LSTM controller could learn to \\"emit\\" reward function subgoals and the VI planner computes how to meet them. A nice/clean division of labor one could hope for in principle.\\r\\n\\r\\n**The experiments**. Unfortunately, I\'m not sure why the authors preferred breadth of exp…718 tokens truncated…ian document lengths are 489.2, 203 words\\r\\n- 30% of the answers in the test set are not in training data answers (i.e. must be \\"read out\\" from the document).\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n#### On a side: related datasets\\r\\n\\r\\n- WIKIQA (Yang et al 2015): only thousands of examples (too small for end-to-end)\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n- NEWS dataset (Hermann et al 2015): 1M instances\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n- bAbI dataset (Weston et al 2015): synthetically generated\\r\\n\\r\\nWIKIQA and NEWS both involve pointing to locations within the document.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Methods: Classification\\r\\n\\r\\nIn this case we have a finite number of possible answers, so there\'s an encoding of item,property to a vector **y** which goes into a Softmax classifier over the finite number of categories.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **BoW baseline**: encode both `item` and `property` to BoW vectors, concat, linear classify to fixed number of answers with Softmax (or Logistic Regression? (since it\'s multi-label setting))\\r\\n- **Neural Net BoW**: embed `item` and `property` by averaging word representations in both separately, concat, classify.\\r\\n- **Paragraph Vector**: encode the item with paragraph vector (Le and Mikolov 2014, PV-DBOW model; an unsupervised method). No fine-tuning throught the model.\\r\\n- **LSTM encoders**: use last hidden representation of an LSTM that \\"read\\" both item/property separately. Presumable these are concatenated into vector **y** that ships off to the Softmax.\\r\\n- **Attentive Reader** from Hermann et al. 2015: Encode the property with an LSTM reader into vector **u**. Then encode the document words into vectors **z**_t using another LSTM. Then produce an attention mask over the document based on concatenation of **(u,z_t)** for all t, and use it to do a weighted sum on **z** to get **r**. Finally, compute the output encoding **y** (which goes into final softmax classifier) with one more layer as a function of **(r,u)**. The concrete equations are: ![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 2.38.24 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 2.38.24 PM.png)\\r\\n  where **v** is a learned vector, so attention is a soft-maxed output of a small 2-layer neural net. Also note to self: isn\'t it a problem that LSTMs are one-directional? what if the the relevant words containing an answer for a property are found preceding the property \\"identifier\\" in text?\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Memory Network** of Sukhbaatar et al 2015, which maps the property **p** and sequence of sentences **x_1, …, x_n** to single joint representation **y** as follows. Each sentence in the item (document) is encoded to a key vector **m** and a content vector **c** and property into a lookup vector **u**. The attention over sentences is computed independently of the property vector, and used to average the content vectors. The output vector **y** is the sum:\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 3.18.05 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 3.18.05 PM.png)\\r\\nNote that this is kind of weird: the document is encoded separately from the query information, and they only interact additively at the very end in Equation (7), and the vector **y** is shipped off directly to the (linear!) classifier. It\'s less intuitive than the Attentive Reader, and will be later shown to also work slightly worse.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Methods: Answer Extraction with \\"RNN Labeler\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nquries that concern date of birth, mother, author etc have too many possible answers to be handled in a classification framework.\\r\\n\\r\\n**RNN Labeler** approach: predict probability of each word being part of the answer. During training annotate document at all occurrences of answer with 1, 0 otherwise. For multi-word answers exact match is required. Instances where answers don\'t appear are discarded. At test: sequences of consecutive locations scoring above a threshold are chunked into single answer, and top-scoring answer is recorded. \\r\\n\\r\\nThis approach is slightly gross, not end to end, and restricted to only predicting words that are verbatim in the document as answers. Also, writeup is a bit vague on how the property is conditioned on in the RNN. Figure 1 seems to suggest that the property is prepended to the document? This seems like a very weak form of conditioning that is bound to fail from the start.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Methods: Answer Extraction with Sequence to Sequence\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Basic seq2seq**: Encode the (item,property) with one LSTM, decode the answer with another in a basic Sutskever et al. Seq2Seq manner. The word embedding is shared but LSTM dynamics aren\'t. The paper is unfortunately very vague here - how are the item and property encoded exactly? Would make sense to maybe encode each, then concatenate? Figure 1 seems to incidate the property is read first and the document next.\\r\\n- **Placeholder seq2seq**: An extension inspired by Luong et al. 2015 / Hermann et al. 2015, where out of vocabulary (OOV) words are replaced at random by one of finite number of placeholder vectors. The softmax word classifier is similarily extended to contain these placeholder words. Just a note: this is really *weird*, since the training has to learn across an entire cross product of placeholder replacements. It feels wrong, but I also can\'t come up with anything much better.=, except for:\\r\\n- **Character seq2seq**: Characters all the way! No such thing as OOV words, weird preprocessing techniques etc., but at the cost of doing much more compute and having much longer dependencies. I like this because the least amount of arbitrary non-differentiable decisions are made.\\r\\n- **Character seq2seq with pretraining**: train a character-level LM on the training data first as initialization (shown as sensible by Dai and Le 2015).\\r\\n\\r\\n ![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.07.18 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.07.18 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nOne more note: these models are suspicious in how lazily they encode the (item, property). It seems they read the property first, and then they read the item for many next time steps, likely nearly forgetting the property by the end. Wouldn\'t it be much more sensible to use very simple attention here, or \\"plug in\\" the property at each time step, or at the last time step etc… many other easy and sensible possibilities here.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Experiements\\r\\n\\r\\n**Eval criterion**: Use Mean F1-score (harmonic mean of precision and recall) due to multiple possible answers; this measures \\"degree of overlap\\" between predicted answer and true answer. Details are a bit sparse here, do they segment multiple answers with e.g. a comma? Since most questions in the dataset have a single answer, F1-score ~= accuracy.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Prepro:** Whoa, \\"all documents are truncated to first 300 words, except in char seq2seq to 400 characters\\" - that is short!. \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Hyperparams:** TensorFlow implementation. Embeddings are 300D. Vocab size 100,000 most freq words. Answer classification is over 50,000 words, \\"answer representation size is 300\\" - wait, is this not a Softmax? RNNs are GRUs with 1024 cells. Opt with Adam of (beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999, eps 1e-8). Grad clipping done proportionally to threhold norm C (not mentioned if seqlength/batches are normalized in loss). Learning rate in 1e-5 to 1e-2, C in [1e-3, 1e1], selected as best from 50.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Results!!** As follows: ![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.22.13 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.22.13 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Attentive Reader works well on cls**: Attentive reader performs best at classification, as it intuitively should imo. I\'m slightly surprised that the LSTM reader performs nearly as well (0.880 vs 0.886) - note it also has fewer params (45M vs 56M).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Order of words has ~little info**: LSTM Reader is 0.880 vs. Averaged Embeddings is 0.849, so order of words information here is adding approx ~0.031of accuracy. This is not a supergreat apples-to-apples comparison though.\\r\\n\\r\\n**More frequent classes work better**, shown in Figure 3. Expected, interesting to see quantitatively. Softmax classifier doesn\'t share statistcal strength across candidate answers. Could have been interesting to maybe model the networks are (item, property, candidate answer) -> probability. This way the answers wouldn\'t blow up the softmax, and inference would be much slower and require a gross loop, but answers could share statistical strength.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Char RNNs works surprisingly well**. Quite surprised to see char seq2seq do 0.699 vs. placeholder seq2seq at 0.718 (and with ~8x less params, but possibly with more FLOPs (would be fun to see this comparison too in the table)). That\'s not a huge delta; encouraging! And this only uses the first 400 characters (instead of 300 words, which should be much more information/context!) of the document and with no attentions/other fanciness. **Pretraining** is mentioned to help with convergence, final performance, and hyperparameter sensitivity.\\r\\n\\r\\n**No attention fancy models for seq2seq**; wish these experiments were included. Would expect an additional bump, as is the case in the categorical setting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Conclusions\\r\\n\\r\\nLets push fully end-to-end character rnn models further. \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE 59 repos/karpathy/pytorch-made/made.py\\r\\n\\"\\"\\"\\r\\nImplements Masked AutoEncoder for Density Estimation, by Germain et al. 2015\\r\\nRe-implementation by Andrej Karpathy based on https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03509\\r\\n\\"\\"\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nimport numpy as np\\r\\n\\r\\nimport torch\\r\\nimport torch.nn as nn\\r\\nimport torch.nn.functional as F\\r\\n\\r\\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\r\\n\\r\\nclass MaskedLinear(nn.Linear):\\r\\n    \\"\\"\\" same as Linear except has a configurable mask on the weights \\"\\"\\"\\r\\n    \\r\\n    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features, bias=True):\\r\\n        super().__init__(in_features, out_features, bias)        \\r\\n        self.register_buffer(\'mask\', torch.ones(out_features, in_features))\\r\\n        \\r\\n    def set_mask(self, mask):\\r\\n        self.mask.data.copy_(torch.from_numpy(mask.astype(np.uint8).T))\\r\\n        \\r\\n    def forward(self, input):\\r\\n        return F.linear(input, self.mask * self.weight, self.bias)\\r\\n\\r\\nclass MADE(nn.Module):\\r\\n    def __init__(self, nin, hidden_sizes, nout, num_masks=1, natural_ordering=False):\\r\\n        \\"\\"\\"\\r\\n        nin: integer; number of inputs\\r\\n        hidden sizes: a list of integers; number of units in hidden layers\\r\\n        nout: integer; number of outputs, which usually collectively parameterize some kind of 1D distribution\\r\\n              note: if nout is e.g. 2x larger than nin (perhaps the mean and std), then the first nin\\r\\n              will be all the means and the second nin will be stds. i.e. output dimensions depend on the\\r\\n              same input dimensions in \\"chunks\\" and should be carefully decoded downstream appropriately.\\r\\n              the output of running the tests for this file makes this a bit more clear with examples.\\r\\n        num_masks: can be used to train ensemble over orderings/connections\\r\\n        natural_ordering: force natural ordering of dimensions, don\'t use random permutations\\r\\n        \\"\\"\\"\\r\\n        \\r\\n        super().__init__()\\r\\n        self.nin = nin\\r\\n        self.nout = nout\\r\\n        self.hidden_sizes = hidden_sizes\\r\\n        assert self.nout % self.nin == 0, \\"nout must be integer multiple of nin\\"\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # define a simple MLP neural net\\r\\n        self.net = []\\r\\n        hs = [nin] + hidden_sizes + [nout]\\r\\n        for h0,h1 in zip(hs, hs[1:]):\\r\\n            self.net.extend([\\r\\n                    MaskedLinear(h0, h1),\\r\\n                    nn.ReLU(),\\r\\n                ])\\r\\n        self.net.pop() # pop the last ReLU for the output layer\\r\\n        self.net = nn.Sequential(*self.net)\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # seeds for orders/connectivities of the model ensemble\\r\\n        self.natural_ordering = natural_ordering\\r\\n        self.num_masks = num_masks\\r\\n        self.seed = 0 # for cycling through num_masks orderings\\r\\n        \\r\\n        self.m = {}\\r\\n        self.update_masks() # builds the initial self.m connectivity\\r\\n        # note, we could also precompute the masks and cache them, but this\\r\\n        # could get memory expensive for large number of masks.\\r\\n        \\r\\n    def update_masks(self):\\r\\n        if self.m and self.num_masks == 1: return # only a single seed, skip for efficiency\\r\\n        L = len(self.hidden_sizes)\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # fetch the next seed and construct a random stream\\r\\n        rng = np.random.RandomState(self.seed)\\r\\n        self.seed = (self.seed + 1) % self.num_masks\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # sample the order of the inputs and the connectivity of all neurons\\r\\n        self.m[-1] = np.arange(self.nin) if self.natural_ordering else rng.permutation(self.nin)\\r\\n        for l in range(L):\\r\\n            self.m[l] = rng.randint(self.m[l-1].min(), self.nin-1, size=self.hidden_sizes[l])\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # construct the mask matrices\\r\\n        masks = [self.m[l-1][:,None] <= self.m[l][None,:] for l in range(L)]\\r\\n        masks.append(self.m[L-1][:,None] < self.m[-1][None,:])\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # handle the case where nout = nin * k, for integer k > 1\\r\\n        if self.nout > self.nin:\\r\\n            k = int(self.nout / self.nin)\\r\\n            # replicate the mask across the other outputs\\r\\n            masks[-1] = np.concatenate([masks[-1]]*k, axis=1)\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # set the masks in all MaskedLinear layers\\r\\n        layers = [l for l in self.net.modules() if isinstance(l, MaskedLinear)]\\r\\n        for l,m in zip(layers, masks):\\r\\n            l.set_mask(m)\\r\\n    \\r\\n    def forward(self, x):\\r\\n        return self.net(x)\\r\\n\\r\\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\r\\n\\r\\nif __name__ == \'__main__\':\\r\\n    from torch.autograd import Variable\\r\\n    \\r\\n    # run a quick and dirty test for the autoregressive property\\r\\n    D = 10\\r\\n    rng = np.random.RandomState(14)\\r\\n    x = (rng.rand(1, D) > 0.5).astype(np.float32)\\r\\n    \\r\\n    configs = [\\r\\n        (D, [], D, False),                 # test various hidden sizes\\r\\n        (D, [200], D, False),\\r\\n        (D, [200, 220], D, False),\\r\\n        (D, [200, 220, 230], D, False),\\r\\n        (D, [200, 220], D, True),          # natural ordering test\\r\\n        (D, [200, 220], 2*D, True),       # test nout > nin\\r\\n        (D, [200, 220], 3*D, False),       # test nout > nin\\r\\n    ]\\r\\n    \\r\\n    for nin, hiddens, nout, natural_ordering in configs:\\r\\n        \\r\\n        print(\\"checking nin %d, hiddens %s, nout %d, natural %s\\" % \\r\\n             (nin, hiddens, nout, natural_ordering))\\r\\n        model = MADE(nin, hiddens, nout, natural_ordering=natural_ordering)\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # run backpropagation for each dimension to compute what other\\r\\n        # dimensions it depends on.\\r\\n        res = []\\r\\n        for k in range(nout):\\r\\n            xtr = Variable(torch.from_numpy(x), requires_grad=True)\\r\\n            xtrhat = model(xtr)\\r\\n            loss = xtrhat[0,k]\\r\\n            loss.backward()\\r\\n            \\r\\n            depends = (xtr.grad[0].numpy() != 0).astype(np.uint8)\\r\\n            depends_ix = list(np.where(depends)[0])\\r\\n            isok = k % nin not in depends_ix\\r\\n            \\r\\n            res.append((len(depends_ix), k, depends_ix, isok))\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # pretty print the dependencies\\r\\n        res.sort()\\r\\n        for nl, k, ix, isok in res:\\r\\n            print(\\"output %2d depends on inputs: %30s : %s\\" % (k, ix, \\"OK\\" if isok else \\"NOTOK\\"))\\r\\n    \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE 60 repos/karpathy/pytorch-made/run.py\\r\\n\\"\\"\\"\\r\\nTrains MADE on Binarized MNIST, which can be downloaded here:\\r\\nhttps://github.com/mgermain/MADE/releases/download/ICML2015/binarized_mnist.npz\\r\\n\\"\\"\\"\\r\\nimport argparse\\r\\n\\r\\nimport numpy as np\\r\\nimport torch\\r\\nimport torch.nn as nn\\r\\nimport torch.nn.functional as F\\r\\nimport torch.optim as optim\\r\\nfrom torch.autograd import Variable\\r\\n\\r\\nfrom made import MADE\\r\\n\\r\\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\r\\ndef run_epoch(split, upto=None):\\r\\n    torch.set_grad_enabled(split==\'train\') # enable/disable grad for efficiency of forwarding test batches\\r\\n    model.train() if split == \'train\' else model.eval()\\r\\n    nsamples = 1 if split == \'train\' else args.samples\\r\\n    x = xtr if split == \'train\' else xte\\r\\n    N,D = x.size()\\r\\n    B = 100 # batch size\\r\\n    nsteps = N//B if upto is None else min(N//B, upto)\\r\\n    lossfs = []\\r\\n    for step in range(nsteps):\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # fetch the next batch of data\\r\\n        xb = Variable(x[step*B:step*B+B])\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # get the logits, potentially run the same batch a number of times, resampling each time\\r\\n        xbhat = torch.zeros_like(xb)\\r\\n        for s in range(nsamples):\\r\\n            # perform order/connectivity-agnostic training by resampling the masks\\r\\n            if step % args.resample_every == 0 or split == \'test\': # if in test, cycle masks every time\\r\\n                model.update_masks()\\r\\n            # forward the model\\r\\n            xbhat += model(xb)\\r\\n        xbhat /= nsamples\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # evaluate the binary cross entropy loss\\r\\n        loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(xbhat, xb, size_average=False) / B\\r\\n        lossf = loss.data.item()\\r\\n        lossfs.append(lossf)\\r\\n        \\r\\n        # backward/update\\r\\n        if split == \'train\':\\r\\n            opt.zero_grad()\\r\\n            loss.backward()\\r\\n            opt.step()\\r\\n        \\r\\n    print(\\"%s epoch average loss: %f\\" % (split, np.mean(lossfs)))\\r\\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------\\r\\n\\r\\nif __name__ == \'__main__\':\\r\\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()\\r\\n    parser.add_argument(\'-d\', \'--data-path\', required=True, type=str, help=\\"Path to binarized_mnist.npz\\")\\r\\n    parser.add_argument(\'-q\', \'--hiddens\', type=str, default=\'500\', help=\\"Comma separated sizes for hidden layers, e.g. 500, or 500,500\\")\\r\\n    parser.add_argument(\'-n\', \'--num-masks\', type=int, default=1, help=\\"Number of orderings for order/connection-agnostic training\\")\\r\\n    parser.add_argument(\'-r\', \'--resample-every\', type=int, default=20, help=\\"For efficiency we can choose to resample orders/masks only once every this many steps\\")\\r\\n    parser.add_argument(\'-s\', \'--samples\', type=int, default=1, help=\\"How many samples of connectivity/masks to average logits over during inference\\")\\r\\n    args = parser.parse_args()\\r\\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------------------\\r\\n    \\r\\n    # reproducibility is good\\r\\n    np.random.seed(42)\\r\\n    torch.manual_seed(42)\\r\\n    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(42)\\r\\n    \\r\\n    # load the dataset\\r\\n    print(\\"loading binarized mnist from\\", args.data_path)\\r\\n    mnist = np.load(args.data_path)\\r\\n    xtr, xte = mnist[\'train_data\'], mnist[\'valid_data\']\\r\\n    xtr = torch.from_numpy(xtr).cuda()\\r\\n    xte = torch.from_numpy(xte).cuda()\\r\\n\\r\\n    # construct model and ship to GPU\\r\\n    hidden_list = list(map(int, args.hiddens.split(\',\')))\\r\\n    model = MADE(xtr.size(1), hidden_list, xtr.size(1), num_masks=args.num_masks)\\r\\n    print(\\"number of model parameters:\\",sum([np.prod(p.size()) for p in model.parameters()]))\\r\\n    model.cuda()\\r\\n\\r\\n    # set up the optimizer\\r\\n    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), 1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)\\r\\n    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(opt, step_size=45, gamma=0.1)\\r\\n    \\r\\n    # start the training\\r\\n    for epoch in range(100):\\r\\n        print(\\"epoch %d\\" % (epoch, ))\\r\\n        scheduler.step(epoch)\\r\\n        run_epoch(\'test\', upto=5) # run only a few batches for approximate test accuracy\\r\\n        run_epoch(\'train\')\\r\\n    \\r\\n    print(\\"optimization done. full test set eval:\\")\\r\\n    run_epoch(\'test\')\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.7 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"5d3c00","wall_time_seconds":0.5348081,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2432,"output":"# Value Iteration Networks\\r\\n\\r\\n**By Berkeley group: Aviv Tamar, Yi Wu, Garrett Thomas, Sergey Levine, and Pieter Abbeel**\\r\\n\\r\\n[Paper link](http://arxiv.org/abs/1602.02867).\\r\\n\\r\\nThis paper introduces a policy network architecture for RL tasks that has an embedded differentiable *planning module*, trained end-to-end. It hence falls into a category of fun papers that take explicit algorithms, make them differentiable, embed them in a larger neural net, and train everything end-to-end.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Observation**: in most RL approaches the policy is a \\"reactive\\" controller that internalizes into its weights actions that historically led to high rewards.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Insight**: To improve the inductive bias of the model, embed a specifically-structured neural net planner into the policy. In particular, the planner runs the value Iteration algorithm, which can be implemented with a ConvNet. So this is kind of like a model-based approach trained with model-free RL, or something. Lol.\\r\\n\\r\\nNOTE: This is very different from the more standard/obvious approach of learning a separate neural network environment dynamics model (e.g. with regression), fixing it, and then using a planning algorithm over this intermediate representation. This would not be end-to-end because we\'re not backpropagating the end objective through the full model but rely on auxiliary objectives (e.g. log prob of a state given previous state and action when training a dynamics model), and in practice also does not work well.\\r\\n\\r\\nNOTE2: A recurrent agent (e.g. with an LSTM policy), or a feedforward agent with a sufficiently deep network trained in a model-free setting has some capacity to learn planning-like computation in its hidden states. However, this is nowhere near as explicit as in this paper, since here we\'re directly \\"baking\\" the planning compute into the architecture. It\'s exciting.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Value Iteration\\r\\n\\r\\nValue Iteration is an algorithm for computing the optimal value function/policy $V^*, \\\\pi^*$ and involves turning the Bellman equation into a recurrence:\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM.png)\\r\\nThis iteration converges to $V^*$ as $n \\\\rightarrow \\\\infty$, which we can use to behave optimally (i.e. the optimal policy takes actions that lead to the most rewarding states, according to $V^*$). \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Grid-world domain\\r\\n\\r\\nThe paper ends up running the model on several domains, but for the sake of an effective example consider the grid-world task where the agent is at some particular position in a 2D grid and has to reach a specific goal state while also avoiding obstacles. Here is an example of the toy task:\\r\\n\\r\\n ![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.43.04 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.43.04 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe agent gets a reward +1 in the goal state, -1 in obstacles (black), and -0.01 for each step (so that the shortest path to the goal is an optimal solution).\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## VIN model\\r\\n\\r\\nThe agent is implemented in a very straight-forward manner as a single neural network trained with TRPO (Policy Gradients with a KL constraint on predictive action distributions over a batch of trajectories). So the only loss function used is to maximize expected reward, as is standard in model-free RL. However, the policy network of the agent has a very specific structure since it (internally) runs value iteration.\\r\\n\\r\\nFirst, there\'s the core Value Iteration **(VI) Module** which runs the recurrence formula (reproducing again):\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 3.26.04 PM.png)\\r\\nThe input to this recurrence are the two arrays R (the reward array, reward for each state) and P (the dynamics array, the probabilities of transitioning to nearby states with each action), which are of course unknown to the agent, but can be predicted with neural networks as a function of the current state. This is a little funny because the networks take a _particular_ state **s** and are internally (during the forward pass) predicting the rewards and dynamics for all states and actions in the entire environment. Notice, extremely importantly and once again, that at no point are the reward and dynamics functions explicitly regressed to the observed transitions in the environment. They are just arrays of numbers that plug into value iteration recurrence module.\\r\\n\\r\\nBut anyway, once we have **R,P** arrays, in the Grid-world above due to the local connectivity, value iteration can be implemented with a repeated application of convolving **P** over **R**, as these filters effectively *diffuse* the estimated reward function (**R**) through the dynamics model (**P**), followed by max pooling across the actions. If **P** is a not a function of the state, it would simply be the filters in the Conv layer. Notice that posing this as convolution also assumes that the env dynamics are position-invariant. See the diagram below on the right:![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.58.42 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 4.58.42 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nOnce the array of numbers that we interpret as holding the estimated $V^*$ is computed after running **K** steps of the recurrence (K is fixed beforehand. For example for a 16x16 map it is 20, since that\'s a bit more than the amount of steps needed to diffuse rewards across the entire map), we \\"pluck out\\" the state-action values $Q(s,.)$ at the state the agent happens to currently be in (by an \\"attention\\" operator $\\\\psi$), and (optionally) append these Q values to the feedforward representation of the current state $\\\\phi(s)$, and finally predicting the action distribution.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Experiments\\r\\n\\r\\n**Baseline 1**: A vanilla ConvNet policy trained with TRPO. [(50 3x3 filters)\\\\*2, 2x2 max pool, (100 3x3 filters)\\\\*3, 2x2 max pool, FC(100), FC(4), Softmax].\\r\\n\\r\\n**Baseline 2**: A fully convolutional network (FCN), 3 layers (with a filter that spans the whole image), of 150, 100, 10 filters. i.e. slightly different and perhaps a bit more domain-appropriate ConvNet architecture.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Curriculum** is used during training where easier environments are trained on first. This is claimed to work better but not quantified in tables. Models are trained with TRPO, RMSProp, implemented in Theano.\\r\\n\\r\\nResults when training on **5000** random grid-world instances (hey isn\'t that quite a bit low?):![Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 5.47.23 PM](img/vin/Screen Shot 2016-08-13 at 5.47.23 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nTLDR VIN generalizes better.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe authors also run the model on the **Mars Rover Navigation** dataset (wait what?), a **Continuous Control** 2D path planning dataset, and the **WebNav Challenge**, a language-based search task on a graph (of a subset of Wikipedia). Skipping these because they don\'t add _too_ much to the core cool idea of the paper.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Misc\\r\\n\\r\\n**The good**: I really like this paper because the core idea is cute (the planner is *embedded* in the policy and trained end-to-end), novel (I don\'t think I saw this idea executed on so far elsewhere), the paper is well-written and clear, and the supplementary materials are thorough.\\r\\n\\r\\n**On the approach**: Significant challenges remain to make this approach more practically viable, but it also seems that much more exciting followup work can be done in this framework. I wish the authors discussed this more in the conclusion. In particular, it seems that one has to explicitly encode the environment connectivity structure in the internal model $\\\\bar{M}$. How much of a problem is this and what could be done about it? Or how could we do the planning in more higher-level abstract spaces instead of the actual low-level state space of the problem? Also, it seems that a potentially nice feature of this approach is that the agent could dynamically \\"decide\\" on a reward function at runtime, and the VI module can diffuse it through the dynamics and hence do the planning.  A potentially interesting outcome is that the agent could utilize this kind of computation so that  an LSTM controller could learn to \\"emit\\" reward function subgoals and the VI planner computes how to meet them. A nice/clean division of labor one could hope for in principle.\\r\\n\\r\\n**The experiments**. Unfortunately, I\'m not sure why the authors preferred breadth of experiments and sacrificed depth of experiments. I would have much preferred a more in-depth analysis of the gridworld environment. For instance:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Only 5,000 training examples are used for training, which seems very little. Presumable, the baselines get stronger as you increase the number of training examples?\\r\\n- Lack of visualizations: Does the model actually learn the \\"correct\\" rewards **R** and dynamics **P**? The authors could inspect these manually and correlate them to the actual model. This would have been reaaaallllyy cool. I also wouldn\'t expect the model to exactly learn these, but who knows.\\r\\n- How does the model compare to the baselines in the number of parameters? or FLOPS? It seems that doing VI for 30 steps at each single iteration of the algorithm should be quite expensive.\\r\\n- The authors should study the performance as a function of the number of recurrences **K**. A particularly funny experiment would be K = 1, where the model would be effectively predicting **V*** directly, without planning. What happens?\\r\\n- If the output of VI $\\\\psi(s)$ is concatenated to the state parameters, are these Q values actually used? What if all the weights to these numbers are zero in the trained models?\\r\\n- Why do the authors only evaluate success rate when the training criterion is expected reward?\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nOverall a very cute idea, well executed as a first step and well explained, with a bit of unsatisfying lack of depth in the experiments in favor of breadth that doesn\'t add all that much.\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"dbbbac","wall_time_seconds":0.2837747,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2547,"output":"# WikiReading paper notes\\r\\n\\r\\nDaniel Hewlett, Alexandre Lacoste, Llion Jones, Illia Polosukhin, Andrew Fandrianto, Jay Han, Matthew Kelcey and David Berthelot, **Google Research**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Pdf link**: http://www.aclweb.org/anthology/P/P16/P16-1145.pdf\\r\\n\\r\\n**Data release link**: http://goo.gl/wikireading\\r\\n\\r\\n18.58M instances across 884 sub-tasks of reading comprehension: text classification, information extraction. Task: predict textual values from **Wikidata** given text **from Wikipedia articles**. Examples form the dataset (cool; wish there were more in appendix or so...):\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 1.53.11 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 1.53.11 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## WikiReading dataset\\r\\n\\r\\n**Wikidata**: 16M items with 80M statements across 844 properties. Each statement is (property, value) tuple. E.g. item Paris has statement (country, France).\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Wikireading**: \\r\\n\\r\\n- Instead consolidate all to (item, property, {answer}), where `item` is replaced with the text of the linked Wikipedia article. \\r\\n- This involves 4.7M unique Wikipedia articles (i.e. ~80% of English Wikipedia is represented). \\r\\n- Most common categories are human, taxon, film, album, human settlement (~50% of docs).\\r\\n- Mean/median document lengths are 489.2, 203 words\\r\\n- 30% of the answers in the test set are not in training data answers (i.e. must be \\"read out\\" from the document).\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n#### On a side: related datasets\\r\\n\\r\\n- WIKIQA (Yang et al 2015): only thousands of examples (too small for end-to-end)\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n- NEWS dataset (Hermann et al 2015): 1M instances\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n- bAbI dataset (Weston et al 2015): synthetically generated\\r\\n\\r\\nWIKIQA and NEWS both involve pointing to locations within the document.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Methods: Classification\\r\\n\\r\\nIn this case we have a finite number of possible answers, so there\'s an encoding of item,property to a vector **y** which goes into a Softmax classifier over the finite number of categories.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **BoW baseline**: encode both `item` and `property` to BoW vectors, concat, linear classify to fixed number of answers with Softmax (or Logistic Regression? (since it\'s multi-label setting))\\r\\n- **Neural Net BoW**: embed `item` and `property` by averaging word representations in both separately, concat, classify.\\r\\n- **Paragraph Vector**: encode the item with paragraph vector (Le and Mikolov 2014, PV-DBOW model; an unsupervised method). No fine-tuning throught the model.\\r\\n- **LSTM encoders**: use last hidden representation of an LSTM that \\"read\\" both item/property separately. Presumable these are concatenated into vector **y** that ships off to the Softmax.\\r\\n- **Attentive Reader** from Hermann et al. 2015: Encode the property with an LSTM reader into vector **u**. Then encode the document words into vectors **z**_t using another LSTM. Then produce an attention mask over the document based on concatenation of **(u,z_t)** for all t, and use it to do a weighted sum on **z** to get **r**. Finally, compute the output encoding **y** (which goes into final softmax classifier) with one more layer as a function of **(r,u)**. The concrete equations are: ![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 2.38.24 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 2.38.24 PM.png)\\r\\n  where **v** is a learned vector, so attention is a soft-maxed output of a small 2-layer neural net. Also note to self: isn\'t it a problem that LSTMs are one-directional? what if the the relevant words containing an answer for a property are found preceding the property \\"identifier\\" in text?\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Memory Network** of Sukhbaatar et al 2015, which maps the property **p** and sequence of sentences **x_1, …, x_n** to single joint representation **y** as follows. Each sentence in the item (document) is encoded to a key vector **m** and a content vector **c** and property into a lookup vector **u**. The attention over sentences is computed independently of the property vector, and used to average the content vectors. The output vector **y** is the sum:\\r\\n\\r\\n![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 3.18.05 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 3.18.05 PM.png)\\r\\nNote that this is kind of weird: the document is encoded separately from the query information, and they only interact additively at the very end in Equation (7), and the vector **y** is shipped off directly to the (linear!) classifier. It\'s less intuitive than the Attentive Reader, and will be later shown to also work slightly worse.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Methods: Answer Extraction with \\"RNN Labeler\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nquries that concern date of birth, mother, author etc have too many possible answers to be handled in a classification framework.\\r\\n\\r\\n**RNN Labeler** approach: predict probability of each word being part of the answer. During training annotate document at all occurrences of answer with 1, 0 otherwise. For multi-word answers exact match is required. Instances where answers don\'t appear are discarded. At test: sequences of consecutive locations scoring above a threshold are chunked into single answer, and top-scoring answer is recorded. \\r\\n\\r\\nThis approach is slightly gross, not end to end, and restricted to only predicting words that are verbatim in the document as answers. Also, writeup is a bit vague on how the property is conditioned on in the RNN. Figure 1 seems to suggest that the property is prepended to the document? This seems like a very weak form of conditioning that is bound to fail from the start.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Methods: Answer Extraction with Sequence to Sequence\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Basic seq2seq**: Encode the (item,property) with one LSTM, decode the answer with another in a basic Sutskever et al. Seq2Seq manner. The word embedding is shared but LSTM dynamics aren\'t. The paper is unfortunately very vague here - how are the item and property encoded exactly? Would make sense to maybe encode each, then concatenate? Figure 1 seems to incidate the property is read first and the document next.\\r\\n- **Placeholder seq2seq**: An extension inspired by Luong et al. 2015 / Hermann et al. 2015, where out of vocabulary (OOV) words are replaced at random by one of finite number of placeholder vectors. The softmax word classifier is similarily extended to contain these placeholder words. Just a note: this is really *weird*, since the training has to learn across an entire cross product of placeholder replacements. It feels wrong, but I also can\'t come up with anything much better.=, except for:\\r\\n- **Character seq2seq**: Characters all the way! No such thing as OOV words, weird preprocessing techniques etc., but at the cost of doing much more compute and having much longer dependencies. I like this because the least amount of arbitrary non-differentiable decisions are made.\\r\\n- **Character seq2seq with pretraining**: train a character-level LM on the training data first as initialization (shown as sensible by Dai and Le 2015).\\r\\n\\r\\n ![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.07.18 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.07.18 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\nOne more note: these models are suspicious in how lazily they encode the (item, property). It seems they read the property first, and then they read the item for many next time steps, likely nearly forgetting the property by the end. Wouldn\'t it be much more sensible to use very simple attention here, or \\"plug in\\" the property at each time step, or at the last time step etc… many other easy and sensible possibilities here.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Experiements\\r\\n\\r\\n**Eval criterion**: Use Mean F1-score (harmonic mean of precision and recall) due to multiple possible answers; this measures \\"degree of overlap\\" between predicted answer and true answer. Details are a bit sparse here, do they segment multiple answers with e.g. a comma? Since most questions in the dataset have a single answer, F1-score ~= accuracy.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Prepro:** Whoa, \\"all documents are truncated to first 300 words, except in char seq2seq to 400 characters\\" - that is short!. \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Hyperparams:** TensorFlow implementation. Embeddings are 300D. Vocab size 100,000 most freq words. Answer classification is over 50,000 words, \\"answer representation size is 300\\" - wait, is this not a Softmax? RNNs are GRUs with 1024 cells. Opt with Adam of (beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999, eps 1e-8). Grad clipping done proportionally to threhold norm C (not mentioned if seqlength/batches are normalized in loss). Learning rate in 1e-5 to 1e-2, C in [1e-3, 1e1], selected as best from 50.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Results!!** As follows: ![Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.22.13 PM](img/wikireading/Screen Shot 2016-08-07 at 4.22.13 PM.png)\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n**Attentive Reader works well on cls**: Attentive reader performs best at classification, as it intuitively should imo. I\'m slightly surprised that the LSTM reader performs nearly as well (0.880 vs 0.886) - note it also has fewer params (45M vs 56M).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Order of words has ~little info**: LSTM Reader is 0.880 vs. Averaged Embeddings is 0.849, so order of words information here is adding approx ~0.031of accuracy. This is not a supergreat apples-to-apples comparison though.\\r\\n\\r\\n**More frequent classes work better**, shown in Figure 3. Expected, interesting to see quantitatively. Softmax classifier doesn\'t share statistcal strength across candidate answers. Could have been interesting to maybe model the networks are (item, property, candidate answer) -> probability. This way the answers wouldn\'t blow up the softmax, and inference would be much slower and require a gross loop, but answers could share statistical strength.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Char RNNs works surprisingly well**. Quite surprised to see char seq2seq do 0.699 vs. placeholder seq2seq at 0.718 (and with ~8x less params, but possibly with more FLOPs (would be fun to see this comparison too in the table)). That\'s not a huge delta; encouraging! And this only uses the first 400 characters (instead of 300 words, which should be much more information/context!) of the document and with no attentions/other fanciness. **Pretraining** is mentioned to help with convergence, final performance, and hyperparameter sensitivity.\\r\\n\\r\\n**No attention fancy models for seq2seq**; wish these experiments were included. Would expect an additional bump, as is the case in the categorical setting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Conclusions\\r\\n\\r\\nLets push fully end-to-end character rnn models further. \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n"}'}]
